paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Vascular Sources The sources of vascular emboli are usually atheromatous plaques in the walls of the aorta, carotid arteries, or smaller vessels in the cerebral circulation. Platelet activation and the formation of a fibrin clot can occur rapidly. The most com-mon areas affected by the emboli of the vascular system are the same as those affected by cardiac sources of emboli. The most common areas for ulcerated plaques in the cerebral blood supply are the aorta and the proximal internal carotid artery. The plaques in the carotid artery can be visualized by Doppler sonography of the carotid artery system. 138

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Paradoxical Sources Congenital atrial septal defects can create the opportunity for emboli to cross from the right-­sided (venous) circula-tion to the left-­sided (arterial) circulation, an uncommon source of cerebral emboli. Paradoxical embolic material can originate from a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). Transesophageal echocardiography with a “bubble study” helps identify patients at risk for this condition. One of the most common atrial shunting abnormalities is a pat-ent foramen ovale (PFO; the fetal opening between the right and left sides of the heart). In young patients or patients who have had TIAs or strokes attributable to a PFO, transcatheter closure of the PFO reduces the risk of subsequent stroke. 147,156,111

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Unknown Sources Thrombi of unknown source often occur in patients with known hypercoagulability syndromes. These syndromes can result from acquired diseases (e.g., lupus anticoagulant and metastatic tumors) or inborn errors of the coagula-tion system (e.g., protein S and C deficiencies). Surgery or medication therapies such as estrogen replacement can induce iatrogenic causes of hypercoagulable states. Even when the patient is known to be in a hypercoagulable state, the source of the emboli may remain unknown. In many patients, the entire workup is unrevealing.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Thrombotic Stroke A thrombotic stroke can result from a variety of causes, but most causes are related to the development of

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: abnormalities in the arterial vessel wall. Atherosclerosis, arteritis, dissections, and external compression of the ves-sels are causes. In addition, some patients with hemato-logic disorders develop thrombosis. The spectrum of disease includes stroke and TIA, and often the difference between a thrombotic and an embolic stroke may be dif-ficult to determine. Thrombosis and embolism are often both present, especially in patients with atherosclerotic disease. The exact mechanism of infarction from throm-bosis is still being debated, but atherosclerosis does play a significant role. Hypertension with associated micro-trauma of the arterial intima is thought to play a role, as is hypercholesterolemia. 138,73 TIAs may result from the formation of microthrombi and their embolization. Large vessel thrombosis can also occur in extracranial vessels, such as the vertebral and carotid arteries, leading to dev-astating strokes. 126 The large vessels are also commonly involved in arterial dissections which are a common cause of stroke among the younger population (patients under 50). In carotid artery dissection a small tear develops in the wall of the artery allowing a thrombus to form. This thrombus can then be a source for emboli, or if large enough occlude the vessel entirely. Dissections can be related to underlying connective tissue diseases like Mar-fan’s or Ehlers Danlos, or can be a result of traumatic inju-ries. Carotid and vertebral artery dissections have been reported not only in high impact trauma such as motor vehicle collisions but also with more minor causes such as cervical chiropractic adjustment, cervical hyperextension while in the hair salon, and hyperextension injuries related to sports. 154

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Atherosclerotic plaque formation is greatest at the branching points of major vessels and forms in areas of turbulent flow. Chronic hypertension is a common pre-cursor, and damage to the intimal wall may be followed by lymphocyte infiltration. Foam cells then develop, and the first stage of atherosclerosis is formed. Calcification and narrowing with resultant turbulent flow follow. In this setting of turbulent flow, plaque ulceration can become a site for thrombus formation. If a thrombus forms and is degraded rapidly, a TIA can occur. Classically, the symp-toms of internal carotid disease include amaurosis fugax, a painless temporary loss of vision, as the ophthalmic artery is a branch off of the internal carotid. If the clot does not break up or lyse, a cerebral infarction can occur. The size and severity of the infarction depend on available col-lateral circulation and the size of the occluded vessel. In patients with extensive atherosclerotic disease, however, a limited amount of collateral circulation is available, and the sparing from collateral circulation may be limited.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Atherothrombotic Disease The most common site for the development of atheroscle-rosis and the subsequent development of atherothrombosis that leads to TIAs and stroke in the anterior circulation is the origin of the carotid artery and in the posterior circula-tion is the top of the basilar artery. Other sites of athero-sclerosis include the carotid siphon and the stems (bases) of the middle cerebral artery, anterior cerebral artery, and origin of the basilar artery. 40 The atheromatous plaques are sources of emboli that can cause distal symptoms in a TIA or stroke. These embolic events are similar events from other embolic sources. Table 1.2 lists common stroke syn-dromes, and Figs. 1.1 to 1.3 explain the anatomy of these strokes. Atherosclerotic disease is screened most readily by carotid Doppler ultrasonography and transcranial Dop-pler imaging. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and carotid and cerebral angiography can further elucidate lesions, which can be treated surgically or medically.
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Lacunar Syndrome A lacunar stroke occurs in one of the perforating branches of the circle of Willis, the middle cerebral artery stem, or the vertebral or basilar arteries. The occlusion of these vessels results from the atherothrombotic or lipohyalinotic blockage of one of these arteries. The development of dis-ease in these arteries correlates closely with the presence of chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular dis-ease. 138,83 These are small vessels, 100 to 300 μm in diam-eter, that branch off the main artery and penetrate into the deep gray or white matter of the cerebrum. 20 The result-ing infarcts are from 2 mm to 3 cm in size and account for roughly 20% of all strokes. These types of strokes usually evolve over a few hours and sometimes can be heralded by transient symptoms in lacunar TIAs. Lacunar strokes can cause recognizable syndromes (Table 1.3). The basic lacunar syndromes are (1) pure motor hemiparesis from an infarct in the posterior limb of the interior capsule or pons, (2) pure sensory stroke from an infarct in the ventrolateral thalamus, (3) ataxic hemiparesis from an infarct in the base of the pons or the genu of the internal capsule, and (4) pure motor hemiparesis with motor apraxia resulting from an infarct in the genu or the anterior limb of the internal cap-sule and the adjacent white matter in the corona radiata. Recovery from a lacunar stroke often can be dramatic, and in some individuals, near complete or complete resolution of deficits can occur in several weeks or months. In patients who have had multiple lacunar infarcts, a syndrome char-acterized by emotional instability, abulia (impairment in or loss of volition), and bilateral pyramidal signs known as pseudobulbar palsy will develop. This diagnosis is based on the symptoms and the use of computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI is especially useful in this situation for detecting small lesions in the deep brain structures or brainstem; the ability of CT to see lesions clearly in these areas is limited. 21

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic Conversion As a sequela of an embolic or ischemic infarction, a purely ischemic infarct may convert into a hemorrhagic lesion.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Thrombi can migrate, lyse, and reperfuse into an isch-emic area, leading to small hemorrhages (petechial hem-orrhages) because the damaged capillaries and small blood vessels no longer maintain their integrity. These damaged areas then can coalesce (combine) and form a hemorrhage into ischemic tissue. 90 These conversions are more com-mon in large infarcts, such as an occluded middle cere-bral artery, or in a large infarction in the distribution of a lenticulostriate artery. In patients who have large infarcts with possibility of hemorrhage, anticoagulation therapy is delayed because of the risk of hemorrhagic conversion. These types of hemorrhages have characteristics in com-mon with hemorrhagic strokes.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic Stroke

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic strokes have numerous causes. The four most common types are deep hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhages (ICHs), ruptured saccular aneurysms, bleed-ing from an arteriovenous malformation (AVM), and spontaneous lobar hemorrhages. 90

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hypertensive Bleed Hypertensive cerebral hemorrhages usually occur in one of four sites: the putamen and internal capsule, pons, thalamus, and cerebellum. Usually these hemorrhages develop from small penetrating arteries in the deep brain that have had damage from hypertension. The usual hypertensive ICH develops over the span of a few minutes but occasionally can take as long as 60 minutes or longer to reach maximal size. Unlike ischemic infarcts, hemor-rhagic bleeds do not follow the anatomic distribution of blood vessels but dissect through tissue planes spherically. This commonly leads to severe damage and complica-tions, such as hydrocephalus and mass shift (movement of brain tissues to one side to accommodate the volume of the hemorrhage). 138,90 Within 48 hours of the hemor-rhage, macrophages begin to phagocytize the hemorrhage at its outer margins. Patients with a cerebral hemorrhage often experience substantial recovery within the first 2 to 3 months after the hemorrhage. ICHs usually occur while patients are awake and may be associated with an episode of emotional distress. Vomiting and headache are asso-ciated commonly with ICH and may help differentiate ICHs from ischemic strokes. Table 1.4 outlines the four major hypertensive ICH syndromes.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Lobar Intracerebral Bleed Lobar hemorrhages are ICHs that occur outside the basal ganglia and thalamus in the white matter of the cerebral cortex. These types of hemorrhages and hypertension are not correlated clearly; the most common underlying con-dition in patients with this type of ICH is cerebral amyloid angiopathy. 27 Other causes include the presence of AVMs, bleeding diatheses, tumors (e.g., melanoma or glioma), aneurysms in the circle of Willis, and a large number of idiopathic cases. 41 Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA)

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: has drawn increased attention in recent years as CAA has shown a clear association with lobar hemorrhage and an increased risk for rebleeding compared to other causes. CAA can be found in any condition that involves the deposition of B-­amyloid in the brain (Alzheimer’s disease) but can also be found in otherwise healthy individuals

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: without cognitive impairment. The amyloid deposits damage the cortical and leptomeningeal vessels predis-posing to hemorrhage. 127 Patients with lobar ICH ini-tially have acute onset of symptoms, and most lobar ICHs are small enough to cause discrete clinical syndromes that may resemble focal ischemic events. Because lobar bleeds occur far from the thalamus and the brainstem, coma and stupor are much less common than they are in patients with hypertensive ICHs. Headaches are also common and can help differentiate lobar bleeds from ischemic strokes, which they can resemble so closely. 137 Detection of a hemorrhage on a CT scan or MRI is the best way to dis-tinguish these two entities.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Saccular Aneurysm and Subarachnoid Bleed A saccular aneurysm rupture is the most common cause of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). 166 Saccular aneurysms occur at the bifurcation (branching) points of the large arteries in the brain and are most commonly found in the anterior portion of the circle of Willis. 11 An estimated 0.5% to 1% of normal individuals harbor saccular aneurysms. 171 Despite the high number, bleeding from them is rare (6 to 16 per 100,000). Unlike other stroke syndromes, however, the incidence of SAH has not declined since 1970. 112 The rupture risk correlates best with the size of the aneurysm. Whereas aneurysms smaller than 3 mm have little chance of hemorrhage, aneurysms 10 mm or larger have the greatest chance of rupture. 72 SAH usually is characterized by an acute, abrupt onset of a severe headache of atypical quality. These headaches are often the most severe that patients have ever experienced. A brief loss of conscious-ness, nausea and vomiting, focal neurologic deficits, and a stiff neck at the onset of symptoms also may occur. The
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, subarachnoid blood found on the CT scan, or blood found in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from a spinal tap. One determines the defini-tive location of the aneurysm by cerebral angiography. Compared to other types of strokes, SAH has a particularly grim prognosis. Although estimates vary, nearly 10-­25% of patients with first time SAH will die before they make it to a hospital. 101 Of those who are admitted, the in-­hospital mor-tality rate is estimated at 18%. Most will die as a result of the initial bleeding but other complications can arise as well. 99 The development of further delayed neurologic deficits results from three major events: rerupture, hydrocephalus, and cerebral vasospasm. Rerupture occurs in 20% to 30% of patients within 1 month if treatment is not aggressive, and rebleeding has an associated mortality rate of up to 70%. 112 Hydrocephalus occurs in up to 20% of patients, and aggressive management often is required. Chronic hydrocephalus is also common and often requires perma-nent CSF drainage (shunting). Vasospasm also is a com-mon problem after SAHs, occurring in approximately 30% of cases. 112 The normal time course for vasospasm is an onset in 3 to 5 days, peak narrowing in 5 to 14 days, and resolution in 2 to 4 weeks. In half of cases, the vasospasm is severe enough to cause a cerebral infarction with resulting stroke or death. Even with modern management, 15% to 20% of patients who develop vasospasms still have strokes or die. 102 A permanent ischemic deficit develops in approxi-mately 50% of patients with symptomatic vasospasms after SAHs. Vasospasm therefore must be treated rapidly and as aggressively as possible to prevent permanent ischemic damage.
cross_page_merge_reasons: medium: unfinished long block continues at the next page

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Arteriovenous Malformation AVMs are found throughout the body and can occur in any part of the brain. They are usually congenital and consist of an abnormal tangle of blood vessels connect-ing arterial and venous systems without an intervening capillary bed. They range from a few millimeters in size to large masses that can increase cardiac output because of the amount of their blood flow. The larger AVMs in the brain tend to be found in the posterior portions of the cerebral hemispheres. 42 AVMs occur more fre-quently in men, and if found in one family member, they have a tendency to be found in other members. AVMs are present from birth, but bleeding most often occurs in the second and third decades of life. Headaches and seizures are common symptoms, as is hemiplegia. Half of AVMs initially present as ICHs. Although rebleed-ing in the first month is rare, rebleeding is common in larger lesions as more time passes. Contrast CT, MRA, and MRI are useful noninvasive tests, and cerebral angi-ography is the best test for delineating the nature of the lesion. For those AVMs that were discovered through medical workup and have not ever bled, evidence sug-gests medical management alone is superior to proac-tive interventional treatment of these AVMs. 119 The management of these lesions once they have bled is accomplished best by a team approach, a combination

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: of surgical treatment and interventional angiography for definitive management. Treatment of hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure (ICP) is the same as treatment for SAH and ICH.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Posttraumatic Hemorrhagic Stroke A traumatic brain injury commonly results in hemorrhagic damage to the brain in addition to ischemic and other injuries. The four major types of injury caused by trau-matic brain injury include SAH and ICH, diffuse axonal injury, contusions, and anoxic injury from hypoperfusion (decreased flow in the vessels) and hypoxemia (decreased oxygen level). This combination of injuries leads to a con-stellation of findings that mixes the features of a number of individual ischemic and hemorrhagic injuries.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Other Causes of Stroke and Stroke-­like Syndromes

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Arterial and Medical Disease Numerous medical conditions can result in arterial system diseases and lead to thrombosis and thromboembolism. Some conditions may cause disease in the cerebral vascu-lature (Table 1.5).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Stroke-­like Syndromes A number of conditions in addition to TIAs and cerebral infarctions can cause transient paralysis. These condi-tions generally resolve spontaneously with no long-­term sequelae. The most common cause of transient hemipa-resis is Todd paralysis, which develops postictally (after a seizure). Todd paralysis results from neurotransmit-ter depletion and neuronal fatigue in focal areas of the brain caused by the extremely high neuronal firing rate during a seizure. 105 Patients usually regain function within 24 hours. Another common cause of focal neu-rologic deficits is migraine headaches. These headaches are actually thought to result from cerebral vasospasms, but an actual ischemic infarct rarely occurs. The deficits
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: resolve with the resolution of the migraine and are not permanent. Another common and quickly reversible cause of neurologic deficits is hypoglycemia. One of the first pieces of information obtained when a person is having symptoms suggestive of a stroke is a point of care blood glucose level. If abnormally low, the patient should be given oral or IV dextrose with reassessment of their symptoms.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Cerebral Neoplasm Cerebral neoplasms (whether primary or metastatic) can lead to focal neurologic deficits that resemble a stroke. The treatment of the sequelae and the long-­term manage-ment of the deficits are similar to stroke patients. Treating the primary lesions is the focus of the acute care. Often the initial symptoms are seizures and ICHs.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: STROKE DIAGNOSIS

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of stroke and differentiation of stroke from strokelike syndromes is based on the clinical presentation and physical examination of the patient. The examiner needs to differentiate a true stroke from syndromes that can mimic a stroke, such as Todd paralysis, seizures, multiple sclerosis, tumors, and metabolic syndromes. Most often, the patient’s symptoms in the emergency department (ED) include an acute onset of weakness or other neurologic deficits. The patient history can help identify the risk fac-tors for stroke and the nature of the lesion. The physical examination includes a general medical examination and a neurologic examination. The National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is a widely accepted assessment tool used to provide a quantitative measure of deficits and describe stroke severity. The scale assesses patients in mul-tiple clinical domains including: consciousness, language, neglect, visual-­ field loss, extraocular movement, motor strength, ataxia, dysarthria, and sensory loss. As well as being a consistent and systematic way of describing stroke deficits, it is also used as a data point in clinical decisions to pursue thrombolytic or interventional management of strokes. Table 1.6 has a full description of the NIHSS. Only after a diagnosis of stroke based on the clinical his-tory and examination can a further diagnostic evaluation be performed. The primary tools available for the accurate diagnosis of stroke are imaging studies, which can identify the exact nature of the lesions causing neurologic deficits.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Each type of imaging has benefits and limitations that are useful to know for assessing a patient who has had a stroke.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Cerebrovascular Imaging

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The main tool used in the initial stroke diagnostic evalua-tions is cerebral imaging. A CT of the brain is the initial and immediate test of choice with other modalities such CT angi-ography and MRI to follow based on the results of the CT.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Computed Tomography CT is a readily available and useful technique that has become the standard for the evaluation of a patient expe-riencing an acute onset of stroke. The most important functions of a CT scan in an acute patient are identify-ing the presence of a hemorrhage (best seen on CT) and ruling out other conditions (e.g., tumor or abscess). In the acute phase of stroke, most CT scans are actually negative with no clear evidence of abnormalities. A nega-tive immediate CT scan with an acute neurologic deficit determined by physical examination actually can verify the impression of stroke because it rules out tumors, hem-orrhages, and other brain lesions. The few changes seen in an acute stroke by CT are subtle and can include loss of distinction between gray and white matter and sulcal effacement. Acute bleeding, however, is easily seen on CT scanning 21. By definition, hemorrhagic infarction occurs within 24 hours of infarction, and hemorrhagic conver-sion occurs after 24 hours of infarction. Hemorrhagic conversion occurs equally in all distributions of infarcts 124 and is not associated necessarily with hypertension or with older age. 56 Hemorrhagic conversion can be detected in the acute phase by CT; in this case, one should not use anticoagulants because they may increase in the severity of the cerebral hemorrhage. CT perfusion studies have been increasingly used as an adjunct to traditional noncontrast CT and CT angiography discussed below to determine the amount of viable tissue surrounding the infarcted area. Perfusion imaging helps delineate the infarcted core and the ischemic but presumably viable surrounding area (penumbra). A patient with a small infarcted core and large ischemic penumbra is likely to benefit most from early reperfusion therapy. In the subacute phase, the findings from CT clearly show the development of cerebral edema within three days, which then fades over the next two to three weeks; then a decrease in the signal intensity occurs over the infarction. This decrease corresponds with the change from the positive mass effect (swelling) of the acute phase to the negative mass effect (shrinkage) of the chronic phase. The infarct actually may be difficult to see again in two to three weeks but is clearly visible with the addition of contrast material. Long-­term parenchymal enhance-ment develops, which is consistent with the scar formation that becomes the permanent CT finding. The loss of tis-sue volume (negative mass effect) and the permanent scar tissue are the characteristic features of a chronic infarct (Figs. 1.4 to 1.8).
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: CT Angiography CT angiography is performed by creating a 3D recon-struction of flow within the blood vessels of the brain after injecting contrast material through a peripheral vein. This helps identify filling defects and any large vessel occlu-sions. As new interventional treatments for acute stroke become more widely accepted, there is a time sensitive need to assess for these large vessel occlusions. When a large vessel is blocked by a thrombus the patient may be eligible for mechanical retrieval of the clot by neuroin-terventionalists. If a large occlusion is suspected, a CT angiogram can be performed immediately after the initial non-­contrast CT of the brain.
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Magnetic Resonance Imaging MRI is now much more commonly used in acute patients in addition to CT because cost and availability have improved. MRI has the advantage of allowing earlier and more sensitive detection of even small infarcts. Image techniques such as diffusion-­weighted imaging help in the identification of early infarcts. 51,157 Magnetic resonance images are created by mapping the relaxation of protons after the imposition of a strong magnetic field. These images are then taken in two primary ways: T1-­ and T2-­ weighted images. In T1 images, fat and tissues with simi-lar proton densities are enhanced (bright). In T2 images, water and tissues rich in water are enhanced. As in CT scans, sulcal effacement can be seen, but hyperintensity is also evident in affected areas on the T1-­weighted images. Magnetic resonance images can show meningeal enhance-ment over the dura, which occurs in 35% of patients with acute stroke. 37 MRI also can detect hemorrhage in much the same way as CT does. MRI studies can be used to

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: estimate the extent of the ischemic penumbra. This infor-mation can be used to help determine if the patient might be a candidate for mechanical thrombectomy, even if outside of the usual time window. Despite MRI’s mul-tiple advantages over CT, the rapidity and simplicity of CT imaging has preserved its role as the initial imaging obtained in most cases of suspected acute stroke or ICH. MRI is able to detect the degradation products of hemoglobin (hemosiderin deposits) and show areas of prior hemorrhage well after CT can no longer detect a bleed. The changes on MRI in a chronic infarction are similar to those on a CT scan.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: WORKUP FOR CAUSE OF STROKE OF TIA

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The workup for the diagnosis of stroke or TIA is aimed at answering three main questions: 1. Is the stroke thrombotic or embolic? 2. Does an underlying cause require specific treatment? 3. Do any risk factors require modification?

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Transcranial and Carotid Doppler

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Transcranial and carotid Doppler studies allow for noninva-sive visualization of the cerebral vessels. The advantages are that they provide useful therapeutic information on the state of the cerebral vessels and the blood flow to the brain. Approx-imately one third of patients who have had ischemic strokes that are cardiac in origin have significant cerebrovascular disease. 104 Patients with symptoms or evidence of posterior circulation disease are tested best with a transcranial Doppler study, including examination of the vertebrobasilar system. The cost is low compared with other tests such as MRA or cerebral angiography. The evidence of carotid disease can help shape the patient’s treatment plan and can encourage pursuit of definitive treatments such as carotid endarterectomy.
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Magnetic Resonance Angiography

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: MRA is used to evaluate patients with stroke symptoms to detect any vascular abnormalities that may have caused the stroke or to look for alterations of cerebral blood flow that may have resulted from an embolic or thrombotic event. This is a very common noninvasive technique and is often done at the time of the MRI scan to assess the extent of cerebral injury; MRA is able to image vessels similarly to classical angiography. 173 The newer techniques of MRA have sensitivity for detection of 86% to 90% 122 for detec-tion of severe stenosis, and the earlier issues of relatively low specificity of 64% 9,86 (because of overdetection by the earlier techniques) is now in the range of 89% to 96% for studies done with contrast-­enhanced MRA. 78 Despite these advantages, the spatial resolution is still less than traditional angiography, which may be an issue in patients in whom surgical management is planned. However, with constantly improving techniques and increased field strengths and parallel imaging, high-­resolution MRA may soon equal the resolution seen in CT angiography. 69

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Electrocardiography

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Electrocardiography (ECG) is used to evaluate patients with stroke symptoms to detect dysrhythmias (which may be a source of embolism) or MI or other acute cardiac events that may be related to an acute stroke. Given that ECG is just a snapshot in time and arrhythmias are often paroxysmal, new techniques which allow for longer term monitoring for dysrhythmias have been adopted. A Holter monitor is a non-­invasive device which is worn for 24-­48 hours and records ECG activity with external skin elec-trodes. For patients whose rhythm will need to be moni-tored longer, an implantable loop recorder may be used. This device is about the size of a USB drive and is inserted just under the skin on the left chest wall. It provides con-tinuous cardiac monitoring and can be left in place for up to 3 years. Unlike a pacemaker or an implantable defibril-lator, the loop recorder is not actually in contact with the heart, but only recording the electrical activity (ECG).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In patients with a history or suspicion of cardiac dis-ease and stroke, echocardiography is usually warranted. The types of cardiac disease that usually cause emboli and should be investigated with an echocardiograph include congestive heart failure (CHF), valvular heart disease, dysrhythmias, and a recent MI. In some indi-viduals, a PFO persists into adulthood and can be the source of a paradoxical embolus from the venous cir-culation that crosses from the right atrium into the left atrium. A transesophageal echocardiogram can then be useful in combination with a bubble study to assess for a right-­to-­left shunt. This specialized study also can visualize parts of the heart better in the search for emboli in areas such as the left atrial appendage or to evaluate the leaflets of heart valves for infective endocarditis when the standard transthoracic echocar-diogram is inconclusive.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Blood Work

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The standard acute evaluation of the stroke patient includes a screening set of blood analyses, including hematologic studies, serum electrolyte levels, and renal (e.g., serum creatinine) and hepatic chemical analyses (liver function tests). The typical hematologic evaluation includes a complete blood count, platelet count, pro-thrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time (PTT). These studies help to rule out other causes of stroke-­like symptoms, to diagnose complications, and to allow for a baseline analysis before the initiation of therapies such as anticoagulation. The blood chemistry analyses allow met-abolic abnormalities to be ruled out, as do the renal and hepatic chemistry analyses. The latter part of the stroke evaluation can involve numerous specialized tests chosen according to the clinical symptoms and development of the differential diagnosis as the evaluation progresses (Fig. 1.9). Table 1.7 provides a sample of some of these studies and their associated conditions.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: MEDICAL STROKE MANAGEMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Principal Goals

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Care for acute patients is provided best in a specialized stroke unit that commonly deals with the issues and con-cerns unique to these patients. 112,1 Outcome studies have demonstrated the benefit of these units in the care of stroke patients. 98 Medical rehabilitation units also have been shown to be beneficial in the improvements of out-comes in the subacute and convalescent phases.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Acute Stroke Management

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In management of acute stroke patients, basic medical needs such as airway protection, maintenance of adequate circulation, and the treatment of any acute concurrent medical problems (e.g. myocardial infarction, dysrhyth-mias) are addressed. The neurologic management of the acute stroke focuses on identifying the cause of the stroke, determining if the patient is a candidate for reperfusion therapy, preventing progression of the lesion, and treating acute neurologic complications.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: General Principles

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The general principles of acute stroke management include attempting to stop progression of the lesion to limit deficits and early reperfusion of ischemic territory, reducing cerebral edema, decreasing the risk of hydro-cephalus, treating seizures, and preventing complications such as DVT or aspiration that may lead to severe illness. After the type of lesion has been defined, specific treat-ment can be instituted. Reperfusion remains a fundamen-tal goal of ischemic stroke management when feasible, using either thrombolytics or mechanical thrombectomy, and reduces both mortality and disability after stroke. Other acute management techniques demonstrated to be beneficial in selected circumstances are surgical evacua-tion of certain types of ICH (e.g. cerebellar hemorrhage causing compression of the fourth ventricle) and decom-pressive craniectomy for impending brain herniation. The basic principles in the approach to the treatment of acute stroke include an attempt to achieve improve-ment in cerebral perfusion by reestablishing blood flow, decreasing neuronal damage at the site of ischemia by modifying the pathophysiological process, and decreas-ing edema in the area of damaged tissue (which often can lead to secondary damage to nonischemic brain tissue). Many pharmacologic and surgical treatments have been targeted toward at least one of these areas. Depending on the stroke mechanism, the agents and techniques of choice are used.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Ischemic Stroke

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In patients who have had ischemic strokes, the restora-tion of blood flow and the control of neuronal damage at the area of ischemia are of the highest priority. In large strokes, edema can play a significant role, and mass effect

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: can lead to brain herniation and death. The pharmaco-logic therapies are divided broadly into antithrombotic, thrombolytic, and anti-­edema therapies. The interven-tional therapies include endarterectomy, stenting, and more recently thrombectomy (mechanical clot retrieval).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Pharmacologic Therapies

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Antithrombotic Therapy (Antiplatelet and Anticoagula-tion). Heparin or other acute anticoagulation is no longer

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: commonly used as a treatment in acute stroke. Aspirin remains a common therapy in acute stroke, but is gener-ally given only after determination by CT or MRI that no hemorrhage is associated with the stroke, and only in patients who are not candidate for reperfusion therapy. While other antiplatelet agents, such as aspirin, Plavix and aspirin-­dipyridamole are used in patients who have had recent strokes and for secondary prevention, their role in acute stroke is not well supported.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Thrombolytic Therapy. Thrombolytic therapy is attrac-tive as a therapy for acute stroke because it restores flow in occluded cerebral vessels and perfusion to ischemic areas. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) has emerged as the thrombolytic agent of choice over the last decade in the US. The mechanism of action is breakdown of fibrin in the clots that have been formed leading to lysis of the occlusion in the blood vessels. The use of thrombolytic treatment has expanded dramatically over the last decade but has been shown to be highly time dependent. At this point, IV tPA is recommended for eligible patients whose last known normal is within 4.5 hours. This time cut-­off has been supported as maximizing therapeutic benefits while balancing the risk of bleeding. Most patients pres-ent outside of this time window, despite ongoing efforts to educate patients regarding the need for acute treatment of possible stroke symptoms. The National Institute of Neu-rological Disorders and Stroke trial was the cornerstone trial in approval of treatment of acute ischemic stroke with thrombolytics. 2,113,58 The trial was a double-­blind, placebo-­controlled trial that revealed an improvement in early outcomes in 24 hours of treatment and demonstrated an increase in symptom-­free survival from 38% (placebo) to 50% (treatment) at 3 months. On reexamination at 1 year, the treated patients continued to show a benefit.95 Later studies specifically the European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study (ECASS) III trial supported safety and effi-cacy out to a 4.5 hour window from last known normal for certain patients. 66 Primary outcome was disability at 3 months. Although IV tPA improved disability at 3 months it did not show a mortality benefit. Unfortunately, the short time window of efficacy limits the number of individuals who can receive benefit of tPA, and the risk of intracranial bleeding after tPA remains a very serious and feared complication. 22,67 In patients with stroke beyond 4.5 hours, direct interventional modalities such as clot retrieval have gained acceptance for selected patients. 113

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Clot Retrieval, Mechanical Thrombectomy Although IV tPA has been widely adopted, it comes with a significant risk of subsequent ICH and has a limited suc-cess rate in reestablishing blood flow in large vessel occlu-sions. These facts along with the narrow therapeutic time window for tPA administration led to the development of endovascular clot retrieval devices. The first clot retrieval device, Mechanical Embolus Removal in Cerebral Isch-emia (MERCI), was approved by the FDA in 2004. Since then, there have been major improvements in technology and an explosion of clinical literature investigating this class of devices and optimizing the indications for their use. Since 2014 there have been nine positive studies showing the mortality and morbidity benefits of mechani-cal clot retrieval in patients with large vessel occlusions. 38 Importantly, patients can be considered as candidates for mechanical thrombectomy regardless of whether or not they received IV tPA. The latest American Heart Associa-tion (AHA) Guidelines on the Early Management of Stroke recommend mechanical thrombectomy for those patients with a large vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation, minimal pre-­stroke disability, NIHSS > 6, within 6 hours of their last known normal. 129 These guidelines expand the use of clot retrieval as “reasonable” out to 24 hours for certain patients based on recent studies which support its safety based on specific patient criteria. 134,64 these cases of delayed intervention, CT perfusion or MRI with diffusion studies are recommended to assess how much viable tissue is left surrounding the obstruction. In this methodology, the emphasis is on the preservation of tissue, rather than an arbitrary cut-­off duration since symptom onset. This measure is known as the ischemic core to viable penumbra ratio and is used as a data point to guide therapy deci-sions. This expanded window out to 24 hours allows for the possibility of transfer to a nearby facility which has the capabilities and expertise for clot retrieval.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Certified Stroke Centers & Mobile Stroke Units Given the time sensitive nature of interventions such as IV tPA and clot retrieval there has been a push to reduce time to intervention. Part of this effort includes the dilemma of whether or not to bypass a nearby hos-pital in favor of transporting a patient to a more distant hospital with interventional capabilities. Hospitals that have acute stroke teams, stroke protocols, stroke units and the ability to administer tPA can be certified as Pri-mary Stroke Centers by the Joint Commission. Those with interventional capabilities and coverage by neuro-interventionalists can garner the Comprehensive Stroke Center certification. Hospitals with these designations demonstrate improved patient outcomes; however, this may be because hospitals who are already prioritizing stroke care are more likely to seek the certification. At this point, although there is no broad mandate for EMS to take patients to a certified stroke center, these protocols are continuing to evolve and in some jurisdictions, such

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: as New York State, there are proposed regulations 183 to require transportation of patients with strokes to Certi-fied Stroke Centers. Another option for improving time to intervention is bringing the hospital team to patients in the field. Mobile stroke units are specially equipped ambulances which include a mobile CT scanner, special-ized staff, lab capabilities and the ability to administer tPA in the field under the telemedicine supervision of a remote neurologist. Mobile stroke units are being trialed as a component of large hospital system stroke care, but are not yet standard of care.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Other Treatments for Altering Cerebral Perfusion A number of different treatments aimed at lowering blood viscosity or cerebral perfusion have been used in the past, including hemodilution with agents such as dextran, albu-min, and hetastarch. None of the 12 studies reviewed by Asplund demonstrated any clear benefit. 5 Similarly, stud-ies of prostacyclins and several different types of cerebral vasodilators have also shown no clear evidence of increased survival rates or improvement in outcomes after treat-ment. 97 Research continues to be active in these areas, but so far none of these alternative treatments for increasing cerebral perfusion has yielded a favorable outcome.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Agents for Cerebral Edema Agents that reduce cerebral edema include corticosteroids, mannitol, glycerol, vinca alkaloids, and piracetam. All the studies done on persons receiving steroids 132 after an acute stroke demonstrated no clear benefits, and steroid use cre-ates a risk of hyperglycemia and DVT. 55 Use of the other agents also has no clear benefit in the treatment of acute stroke, so they are also not routinely used. Interventions for cerebral edema are typically limited to elevating the head of the bed, monitoring serum electrolytes, and neu-rosurgical intervention if cerebral edema is so severe as to necessitate direct reduction of intracranial pressure.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Cooling Therapy Another proposed treatment of acute stroke has been the initiation of cooling therapy on presentation with the induction of a medical coma to limit the extent of brain injury after stroke. In most patients who present with stroke, there is a natural tendency for the body temper-ature to be elevated between, which is associated with increased injury and poorer outcomes. 12,29 Induction of hypothermia has shown some promise in post cardiac arrest patients who do not quickly regain consciousness when they achieve return of spontaneous circulation, and is now included in the most recent Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) guidelines. Despite success in post arrest patients, existing studies on the application of mechani-cal or pharmacologic cooling of acute stroke patients do not yet provide convincing evidence that death or long-­ term disability is significantly reduced. We do, however, know that temperature management and treating elevated body temperature and maintaining normothermia reduces cerebral oxygen demand and is part of standard stroke unit care.
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Surgical Therapies Endarterectomy. A carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is the surgical opening of the carotid arteries to remove plaque and restore flow. This therapy has been shown to be use-ful in preventing recurrent strokes or development of stroke in individuals with TIAs, but it has not been used to treat acute stroke. In theory, the opening of the carot-ids could subject ischemic areas and their blood vessels to excessive pressure from restored blood flow and lead to hemorrhage. 118 Concerns about using major anesthesia in a patient with an acute stroke makes this surgery too risky to treat acute stroke. However CEA is routinely used in stroke prevention. The North American Symptomatic Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) showed the 2 year stroke risk for patients with symptomatic >70% occlusions were 26% with medical management versus 9% with sur-gical management (CEA). 69 Currently the indication for a carotid endarterectomy includes 70% or greater stenosis of the carotid artery with symptoms including prior ipsi-lateral stroke or TIA. A patient is not a candidate for a CEA if there is 100% occlusion. The reasoning is there is already collateral blood flow perfusing that region and the surgery would be technically too risky as there would be no way to pass a filter upstream of the lesion to catch emboli as the plaque is removed.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Balloon Angioplasty & Endovascular Stents. Given its effi-cacy in opening blocked coronary arteries in patients with heart disease and its successful treatment of acute MI, the use of balloon angioplasty has been explored in stroke as well. Although angioplasty and endovascular stents are not typically used in acute stroke, but have emerged as viable options for stroke prevention. Most commonly endovascular stents are deployed to open the stenotic internal carotid arteries. However, they can also be used for other vessels including the basilar artery. The Carotid Revascularization Endarterectomy versus Stenting Trial (CREST) trial in 2012 compared carotid endarterec-tomy to stenting and found them comparable in efficacy and complications. 17 Given the non-­inferiority of stent-ing, the less invasive procedure is gaining traction as a treatment.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic Stroke

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In patients who have had a hemorrhagic stroke, the size and location of the lesion determine the overall prognosis; supratentorial lesions larger than 5 cm have a poor prog-nosis, and brainstem lesions larger than 3 cm are usually fatal. 41 In these cases, the control of edema is important, and the techniques previously described can be used. In patients with SAH, the treatment regimen is usually more aggressive and focuses on several issues, which include the

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: control of ICP, prevention of re-­bleeding, maintenance of cerebral perfusion, and control of vasospasm.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Prevention of Re-­bleeding Before 1980, 6 weeks of bed rest was prescribed routinely for the care of patients with acute SAH to prevent re-­ bleeding. In 1981, a study demonstrated that bed rest was inferior to surgical treatment, lowering of blood pres-sure, and carotid ligation. 171 Carotid ligation has been largely abandoned because of its surgical risks and the advent of techniques for direct repair of the aneurysm including clipping and endovascular coiling. Only treat-ment of the aneurysm itself has been shown to be effec-tive in preventing re-­bleeding. In aneurysmal clipping an extraluminal clip is placed at the base of the aneurysm causing occlusion. Endovascular coiling involves the placement of platinum coils into the lumen of the aneu-rysm. These coils become a nidus for thrombus forma-tion which occludes the area of the aneurysm. Aneurysms treated with clipping have a lower rate of recurrence and need for repeat intervention. 81,120 The timing of surgical intervention after the rupture of an aneurysm is contro-versial and still an area of active research. Antifibrinol-ytic agents have been studied and have been beneficial for low-­risk patients in whom surgery must be delayed, but they seem to increase the risk of ischemic events. 112 Because the risk of re-­bleeding is also very high in post-­ SAH seizures, even though the incidence of seizure is low, the recommendation is that patients receive antisei-zure medications for prophylaxis.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Control of Vasospasm The treatment of vasospasm is important to pre-vent ischemic stroke as a complication of SAH. Cur-rent treatments include the use of orally administered nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker shown to improve outcomes of patients who have had an SAH with vasospasm. Nimodipine is administered within the first 4 days of SAH and continued for 21 days. The use of hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution was initially recommended by some studies. Creating more volume than normal results in hypertension and stimulates the smooth muscle pressure receptors that line the vessels. These receptors inhibit muscle action by a protective response, and the blood vessel dilates to accommodate the increased volume. The combina-tion of hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution was thought to prevent vasospasm after surgically clip-ping the aneurysm. However, current guidelines favor euvolemia with systolic blood pressure between 140-­ 160. Because nimodipine in such high doses can signifi-cantly reduce the blood pressure, patients sometimes need additional medications to augment their blood pressure. Significant cardiac and hemodynamic risks are associated with this therapy, so intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring is required. 112

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: PREVENTION OF STROKE RECURRENCE

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Ischemic Stroke

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In general, the strategies to prevent recurrence of isch-emic stroke involve targeting and modifying the same risk factors involved in primary prevention which in some cases include the treatment of an underlying medical con-dition (arrhythmia, hyperlipidemia, atherosclerosis et al).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hypertension Diastolic and systolic hypertension are each independently and strongly implicated in causing stroke. Hypertension increases the risk of stroke in all age groups of men and women. 180 In fact, no threshold level of blood pressure exists below which the risk curve plateaus. 107 For every 7.5–mm Hg increase in diastolic pressure is a 46% increase in stroke incidence and a 29% increase in coronary heart disease (CHD). Reducing blood pressure in hypertensive patients has been shown to decrease the risk of stroke sig-nificantly, with an average reduction of 5.8 mm Hg lead-ing to a reduction in stroke incidence of 42% but only a 14% reduction in CHD incidence. 26 Because these trials only spanned 2 to 5 years, the reduction in stroke inci-dence is a direct result of decreased blood pressure and not an alteration in atherogenesis (production of plaque in the arteries), which would take longer to develop. 180 Sys-tolic blood pressure is also a factor; the treatment of iso-lated systolic hypertension (>160 mm Hg) has been shown to reduce the incidence of stroke by 36% and CHD by 27% over 4.5 years. 60 Treating all forms of hypertension in the older age groups is therefore essential because they are at increased risk for stroke, and most strokes occur in this age group. Screening for hypertension and aggres-sively treating systolic and diastolic hypertension should be the cornerstone of any primary prevention program for stroke. Control of hypertension immediately following a stroke and in the chronic setting is also important. The transient rise in blood pressure after stroke usually settles without intervention. 19 In fact elevation of blood pressure in the acute setting is acceptable and even favorable. A patient who has lived at a very high systolic pressure lead-ing up to the stroke, will likely need that higher pressure to maintain perfusion of the remaining viable tissue (isch-emic penumbra). The current recommendations favor permissive hypertension up to 220/105 for the first 24 hours, then up to 180 systolic for the first two weeks. 129 After two weeks, one should aim for chronic control less than 140/80. A multicenter, international trial random-ized patients with previous stroke in the last 5 years to treatment with an antihypertensive or placebo. The rela-tive risk reduction of recurrent stroke at 5 years was 28% and even higher for those with previous ICH. 59 This study among others highlights the importance of long-­term BP control for secondary prevention.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hyperlipidemia Strokes are a well-­established complication of athero-sclerotic disease and the development of atherosclerotic disease in the carotid arteries as well as other vascula-ture has been shown to be related to the levels of serum lipids. 144 The treatment of hyperlipidemia through the use of statins has been used successfully for pri-mary prevention of stroke in patients with risk factors for cerebrovascular disease. 142,62 Low density lipopro-tein (LDL) cholesterol has been specifically targeted as being associated with the development of clinically significant atherosclerotic disease. Recommendations center around the reduction of LDL specifically, with target levels depending on cardiovascular risk. More recent evidence suggests statin therapy is also beneficial in secondary prevention and recurrence of strokes. The Stroke Reduction by Aggressive Reduction of Choles-terol Levels (SPARCL) trial showed a 16% reduction of fatal or non-­fatal stroke at 5 years for those patients tak-ing a high dose statin (Atorvastatin 80mg daily) versus placebo. 79 Statins even reduce the risk of stroke in high risk patients with normal or below average cholesterol arguing for treatment of a larger cohort of patients with significant stroke risk factors. 151

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Diabetes The rate of atherosclerosis development in coronary, femoral, and cerebral vessels is increased in patients with diabetes. Stroke is increased 2.5 to 4 times in patients with diabetes compared with those without diabetes. 94 In the Framingham Study, glucose intolerance (blood sugar >150 mg/mL) is only a significant, independent contribu-tor to stroke in older women and is greater for women than men at any age. 87 Because of the associated risk of stroke, careful management of diabetes in addition to all other risk factors is prudent.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Oral Contraceptives In women older than age 35 years who have other stroke risk factors, oral contraceptive use is associated with an increased incidence of stroke. 18 The relative risk for oral contraceptive users is approximately five times greater if they are already in the high-­risk group. With the use of lower estrogen oral contraceptives, the risk has decreased substantially in recent years. 159 That the incidence of fatal SAH increased in oral contraceptive-­using women with concomitant smoking is noteworthy; in the group older than age 35 years, the incidence is four times higher. 162 Therefore, the recommendation is that women older than the age of 35 years avoid using oral contraceptives, and younger women who smoke should be advised of the increased risks associated with concurrent oral contracep-tive use. Although the pathophysiology is still not well understood, women who have migraines with aura are at an increased risk for stroke. This risk is even higher when these women take combined OCPs. However, despite the increased risk, the absolute risk is still quite low and migraines are not an absolute contraindication to the use of OCPs. 152
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Lifestyle Modification (Activity, Alcohol Consumption, Smoking) General lifestyle modification including exercise, limiting alcohol consumption and avoiding or quitting smoking have clear benefits for reducing risk of stroke. Although weight loss and exercise have been clearly associated with a reduction in heart disease morbidity and mortality, the link to stroke is not as well established. Even with limited evi-dence linking these particular behavioral changes to stroke, encouraging a healthier diet and addressing obesity affects other cardiovascular risk factors including hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and is an important part of post-­stroke counseling. The AHA and American Stroke Association (ASA) both recommend weight loss for patients who are overweight or obese as a general strategy for health. Heavy alcohol consumption is related to an increase in stroke and stroke deaths, although light to moderate alco-hol consumption is associated with a reduced incidence of CHD. 33,93 Alcohol is clearly related to hemorrhagic stroke events, but the association with thromboembolic events is not definite. Regardless, patients at risk for stroke should avoid heavy alcohol consumption. The results of the Framingham Study and the Nurses’ Health Study demonstrate that the cessation of cigarette smoking should lead to a prompt reduction in stroke mor-tality. 23,182 The risk of CHD decreases by 50% in 1 year and reaches the level of a nonsmoker’s risk in 5 years. Smoking increases stroke risk by 40% in men and 60% in women (with no other risk factors being considered), and smoking cessation is an essential component of secondary stroke prevention.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Antiplatelet Medications In patients who have had a TIA or stroke, long-­term use of aspirin has been shown to decrease the incidence of death, MI, and recurrent events by up to 23%. 24 The doses of aspirin used across numerous studies have ranged from 30 mg to 600 mg; all doses resulted in a 14% to 18% reduction in recurrent cerebral events, but gastrointesti-nal complications increased with the higher doses. 61,39,63 In general, the standard dosage of one baby aspirin (81 mg/day) is the usual treatment for recurrent ischemic stroke. Multiple other antiplatelet agents have arisen in recent years as alternatives or additions to aspirin. Most commonly used are clopidogrel (Plavix) and dipyridam-ole. Many studies have examined the benefits of adminis-tration and duration of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) combining aspirin with clopidogrel or dipyridamole. The antiplatelet effect and reduction in recurrent stroke must be balanced by the increased risk for bleeding. In the short term after an acute ischemic stroke, the combination of these agents reduces the risk of recurrent stroke. The

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: exact length of time to continue DAPT is still being deter-mined. Two large prospective trials suggest 30 days of two agents reduces the risk of major ischemic events with only a small increase in clinically significant bleeds. 82,176 Tri-als are ongoing to examine the optimal duration of dual treatment and treatment is highly provider and institution dependent, but at present, dual antiplatelet therapy is rec-ommended for 30 days following an acute stroke and then followed with a single antiplatelet agent.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Anticoagulation The risk for stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation is approximately 5 fold higher than those without. Those patients who have already had a stroke and remain untreated for atrial fibrillation have an estimated risk of recurrent stroke per year of 2.2% to greater than 10% based on other risk factors. 43 Factors that increased risk in the large Swed-ish Atrial Fibrillation Cohort Study include gender (female), hypertension, diabetes, CHF, and age. For patients who have atrial fibrillation with cardiac sources of emboli, full anticoagulation is the treatment of choice; this is true for pri-mary and secondary prevention. Although warfarin remains an appropriate treatment option, it is gradually being sup-planted by the Novel Oral Anticoagulants (NOACs) also termed direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). These drugs do not require monitoring with serial blood tests and do not require diet adjustments as warfarin does. Though ini-tially marketed as non-­inferior to warfarin in the reduction of stroke risk for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, the most recent guidelines by the AHA, American College of Car-diology (ACC) and Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) suggest NOACs have a superior risk/benefit profile. 155 This shift in recommendation comes in part following the development and distribution of reversal agents for specific NOACs in the event of uncontrolled bleeding. The risk of stroke has to be balanced with the risk of bleeding which in many elderly patients is significant. Multiple clinical decision instru-ments exist to quantify these risks. Unless the patient has an extremely large ischemic stroke prone to hemorrhagic con-version, anticoagulation is typically started within 48 hours of a stroke if Afib is judged to be the cause. For warfarin the goal international normalized ratio (INR) is typically between 2 and 3 for nonvalvular Afib.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Carotid Endarterectomy Carotid stenosis is often discovered in the evaluation for the cause of a stroke. Routine screening for carotid disease is not recommended, however. The surgical treatment of carotid artery stenosis has been shown to be beneficial in recent studies of stroke recurrence in patients with severely (>70%) stenosed carotid arteries. 25,57 For patients with high-­grade stenosis, CEA reduces the range of stroke risk from 22% to 26% down to 8% to 12%. Patients with com-plete occlusions are not candidates for surgery or stenting of the occluded carotid. As discussed previously carotid stenting is also an option and has been proven as effective as CEA. If in the course of other medical treatment a patient is found to have asymptomatic carotid stenosis, treatment course is less definitive. For asymptomatic patients the periprocedural risks of intervention are often higher than treatment with medical therapy. 158 With the development of large registries of patients with asymptomatic carotid stenosis, guidelines for invasive intervention are evolving.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic Stroke

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The mainstay of ICH prevention is controlling systolic and diastolic hypertension. No clear benefit exists for one group of treatment agents versus another as long as adequate hypertension control is maintained. In patients in whom the ICH follows vasculitis or the use of antico-agulants, the treatment for preventing recurrence includes treating the vasculitis or terminating anticoagulant use. 138 The secondary prevention of recurrent stroke and SAH of AVMs or aneurysms includes surgical management of the lesions (the treatment of choice). Clipping or micro-surgical dissection of the lesions is performed whenever possible and as soon as the patient is able to safely undergo the procedure. 112,165 In surgically unresectable lesions, alternatives include sclerotherapy, coating, trapping, and proximal arterial occlusion. 112

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: PREVENTION OF COMPLICATIONS AND LONG-­TERM SEQUELAE

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: General Principles

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: To prevent complications and long-­term sequelae after a stroke, maximizing function, decreasing morbidity, and preventing rehospitalization from a complication are important. Prevention of these complications begins on the day the patient arrives at the hospital with symptoms of acute stroke. Many complications are associated with bed rest in general, but some are specific to stroke.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Musculoskeletal Complications

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Contractures Contractures are periarticular motion impairments that result from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues, which include muscles, tendons, and ligaments. Con-tractures can occur in any immobilized joint but are particularly prevalent in paretic limbs after a stroke. In fact, only 10% of hemiplegic stroke patients recover limb strength and mobility rapidly enough to avoid devel-oping contractures 65 Shoulder pain, contractures, and muscle pain occur in 70% to 80% of patients who have had a hemiplegic stroke. 9 Chapter 20 addresses the man-agement and related issues of the hemiplegic shoulder. Contractures also occur in other areas and begin to be problematic within a few days of onset or several days after the stroke when symptoms of immobility and spas-ticity may begin to develop. Usually contractures occur in a pattern of flexion, adduction, and internal rotation; muscles that span two joints are more susceptible to

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: contracture formation. 70 To prevent shortening of the connective tissue in muscles and joints, an active range of motion (ROM) program must be initiated. Because cer-tain muscles span two joints, joints must be positioned to allow full physiological stretch of the muscles involved. When a contracture is present, the mainstay of treatment is gradual, prolonged stretch. The minimal treatment is a sustained stretch greater than 30 minutes. 92 Other treat-ments include splinting, deep-­heating modalities, 135 and possible surgical release for long-­standing, severe con-tractures 107 (see Chapter 23).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Osteoporosis Bone is a metabolically active tissue normally in a state of equilibrium between active bone resorption and deposi-tion. The ratio of bone formation to bone resorption is influenced by the stressors to which the bone is subjected, a relationship known as Wolff’s law. 135 The lack of weight bearing and normal stress on long bones on the hemiple-gic side of a stroke patient leads to a predominance of bone resorption. This loss of bone mass can start as early as 30 hours after the beginning of immobility 170 and with bed rest can be as high as 25% to 45% in 30 to 36 weeks. 34 In patients who have had a stroke, osteoporosis is often worse, and the rate of hip fracture is far higher on the side of the hemiplegia. Osteoporosis can not currently be completely pre-vented, but can be mitigated with measures that include active weight-­bearing exercise and active muscle contrac-tion. Medical therapies for individuals at risk for osteopo-rosis should be initiated. Therapies include bone-­forming agents, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, hormone replacement, and other measures as needed. Box 1.1 shows some of the medical treatments available for osteoporosis.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Falls Falls are of particular concern in survivors of stroke. These patients are at increased risk of hip fracture because of developed osteoporosis, and the acuity of their balance, visual perceptions, and spatial perceptions are decreased. The increased risk of falls has been documented in several studies and is greater in patients who have had a right hemi-spheric stroke. 130,117,128 Fall prevention should emphasize balance and cognitive training, removing environmental hazards, and using adaptive devices. (These measures are reviewed in Chapters 6, 17, 18, 19, 26, and 30.)

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Neurologic Complications

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Seizures Seizures after strokes have been documented since the 19th century. Whereas the incidence of late-­onset seizures (epi-lepsy) in individuals who have had strokes ranges from 6% to 18%, 52,71,175 the incidence of early seizures is approxi-mately 10%, with reports ranging from 3% to 38%. 10,179 The risk for seizures is highest right after stroke: 57% of seizures occur in the first week, and 88% of all seizures after stroke occur in the first year. 10 Seizures are more common in patients who have had any type of hemorrhagic stroke; 85% of these seizures are early seizures. 164 The timing of seizures that occur after stroke varies according to the mechanism of injury. The timing of seizures after throm-botic and embolic strokes appears about equal. Whereas patients with SAH have more seizures soon after the stroke, patients with ICH are more similar to patients with ischemic stroke and may have more late-­onset seizures. 179 The treatment and management of seizures associated with stroke are usually straightforward, and monotherapy often produces adequate results. Routine medication for seizure prophylaxis after a stroke is not recommended. If the patient only has acute-­onset seizures in the setting of his or her stroke, the patient often does not require long-­ term antiseizure medication. A single, brief seizure or a nongeneralizing local seizure also can often be managed conservatively. If seizures do require treatment, a single agent usually suffices and is beneficial because the drug interactions are fewer, and the compliance is better with monotherapy. Levetiracetam (Keppra) is the preferred initial agent for treating seizures after stroke in most patients. Among other advantages over older anticon-vulsants, Levetiracetam does not typically require moni-toring of blood levels. All seizure medications can have side effects (Box 1.2). Table 1.8 lists the common seizure medications and their side effects.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Hydrocephalus Hydrocephalus can occur acutely, especially in patients with SAH and ICH as discussed previously, or it can develop insidiously later. Hydrocephalus is usually her-alded by the gradual onset of a triad of symptoms, includ-ing lethargy with decreased mental function, ataxia, and urinary incontinence. When hydrocephalus is suspected, one should perform a CT scan promptly, demonstrated ventricular enlargement in this condition. Treatment typ-ically involves surgical placement of a ventricular shunt. The procedure is well tolerated and can lead to resolu-tion of all the symptoms of hydrocephalus if performed promptly. Patients with an occluded shunt have symptoms that mimic the initial symptoms of hydrocephalus.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Spasticity Spasticity is defined as a motor disorder characterized by a velocity-­dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes with exaggerated tendon jerks. Spasticity results from

paragraphs.text: • Irritability

paragraphs.text: • Poor cognition
