paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: ponent of the upper motor neuron syndrome). 84 In a typi-cal pattern of recovery after hemiplegic stroke, an initial period occurs with little resistance to passive motion of the muscles and joints. Approximately 48 hours after the stroke, tendon reflexes and muscle resistance to passive motion begin to return. 70 Whereas the lower extremity usually develops extensor spasticity that can assist with function, the upper extremity spasticity is usually in a flexor pattern. 125 The management of spasticity includes encouraging voluntary movement, ROM exercises, and a functional rehabilitative approach (see Chapter 20). 70 Oral medi-cations include baclofen, dantrolene sodium, and diaz-epam. Unfortunately, many stroke survivors are unable to tolerate these medications at effective doses due to sedation and adverse cognitive effects. Injection therapy with botulinum toxin (Onabotulinum toxin and others) is widely used for focal spasticity, and is highly effective and well tolerated. 32,88,48 Other treatments for severe spas-ticity include phenol or ethanol neurolysis and implant-able baclofen pumps. Intrathecal baclofen pumps show good efficacy but are an invasive treatment and typically reserved for unusually severe spasticity. 28

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Post Stroke Pain Pain following a stroke can be secondary to musculoskele-tal, mechanical complications as discussed previously or as a result of damage to the central nervous system. Central pain from a stroke typically presents 1-­2 months after the event with burning, tingling, radiating pain. This type of pain affects approximately 10% of stroke survivors and is most common in patients whose strokes affected areas of the CNS carrying sensory pathways. Post stroke central pain syndrome (PSCPS) is classically described due to thalamic stroke, but can originate from damage to sensory tracts throughout the CNS. The pathophysiology of PSCPS has not been entirely elucidated. Most treatments target neuro-nal hyperexcitability. Success with tricyclic antidepressants and anticonvulsants suggest both sodium channels and cal-cium channels play a part in modulating this pain. Trials of multiple different medications may be needed, and treat-ment is often unsatisfactory in this condition. A second recognized syndrome of post stroke neuro-pathic pain is complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). The reported incidence of CRPS is widely variable. Pub-lished rates range from 2% to nearly half of all stroke patients 114,91 but the lower figures appear more consistent with contemporary clinical experience in the US. Some of this discrepancy likely results from varying diagnostic cri-teria and the challenge in differentiating this type of pain from other post stroke pain syndromes. This syndrome most commonly affects the upper extremity and involves an evolution of severe pain accompanied by vasomotor changes (sweating, increased blood flow) in the affected arm eventually changing over months and years to atrophy, and loss of range of motion in that limb. Although the exact mechanism of CRPS is not known, the pain is thought to be mediated by the sympathetic nervous system given the multiple downstream autonomic effects (sweating, redness, increased blood flow). It seems early mobilization helps

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: prevent this complication. No single drug is approved to treat CRPS, but a combination of antidepressants, steroids for inflammation, topical anesthetics and systemic analge-sics are used for management. In some severe cases a sym-pathetic nerve block can be performed by an interventional pain specialist for both diagnostic and therapeutic effect.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Other Complications

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Deconditioning Physiological deconditioning in patients after a stroke results from the acute medical illness and the associated bed rest and immobility that may result. Table 1.9 lists some of the effects of deconditioning. All of these factors can alter the ability of the patient to recover. Therefore, it is important to get the patient out of bed early post-­ stroke, and to increase activity steadily. Very aggressive early mobilization after stroke (within the first day after stroke) should be avoided due to concern that this may actually contribute to worse outcomes. 8

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Psychological Complications Stroke is a major life event and is associated with signifi-cant alterations in the individual’s well-­being and inde-pendence. Negative emotional reactions are common in patients after a stroke 168 and can have a significant effect on the patient’s eventual outcome. After a stroke, patients may go through the four stages of bereavement described by Worden. 85 These include accepting the loss, experienc-ing the pain of the loss, adjusting to a new environment in which previous abilities are missing, and investing in new activities. Depression is extremely common post stroke with estimates ranging from 20-­ 50%. A recent meta-­ analysis estimated approximately a third of stroke survi-vors will have a major depressive episode in the 5 years after stroke. 68 This consequence seems tied not only to loss of function and adjustment to a disability, but also to underlying changes in the brain. The rates of depression in stroke survivors are higher than for similar groups who have dealt with non-­neurologic traumatic incidents such as amputations. The consequences of depression after stroke are numerous: hospital stays are longer 141,cognitive impairment is greater, 136 and motivation decreases. 153 Depression after stroke typically responds well to anti-depressant medications. 168 In patients who are unable to tolerate antidepressants, are unresponsive to therapy, or have active suicidal ideation, electroconvulsive therapy may be considered. 121 (See Chapter 15 for more informa-tion about the psychological effects of stroke.) Another common consequence of stroke is emotional lability, which is rapidly shifting from one extreme emo-tion to another. Approximately 20% of patients have emo-tional lability 6 months after a stroke, and up to 10% have lability at 1 year. Emotional lability is more common in patients with pseudobulbar palsy and right hemispheric strokes, particularly if the patient is depressed. 77 The FDA has approved one medication specifically for the treat-ment of pseudobulbar palsy; Nuedexta is a combination of dextromethorphan and quinidine. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are also often used with some success. Treatment also includes education and reassur-ance of the patient and family that this is a known and common part of the disease process. Anxiety is also common after stroke and is more frequent in patients with left hemispheric strokes 115 and cortical lesions. 160 Many sources of anxiety exist, including finan-cial affairs, family issues, and a fear of dying or recurrent stroke. Reassurance and positive feedback during rehabili-tation can help, and in more severe cases, treatment with psychotherapy and/or anxiolytics may be needed.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Urinary Tract Dysfunction Urinary incontinence is common after stroke, affecting 51% to 60% of patients, 14 and can cause difficulties with rehabilitation, influence eventual discharge location, and place stress on caregivers. 36 One month and 6 months after stroke, 29% and 14% of patients, respectively, still have urinary incontinence. 31 The usual pathophysiology of incontinence is detrusor hyperreflexia, which is com-mon in patients with cortical lesions. A stroke damages the inhibitory pathways that modulate micturition. The lack of inhibitory input results in repeated spasms of the detrusor muscle creating a feeling of urgency as well as contributing to incontinence. Initial treatment can begin with conservative approaches such as more frequent uri-nation and limiting fluid intake before activity. If phar-macologic intervention is needed, anticholinergics are

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: effective. However, anticholinergics come with a host of side effects (dry mouth, confusion, constipation, sedation) and many patients discontinue them for this reason. If oral medications fail to control symptoms, botulinum toxin injection is an option for managing the muscle spasms. In more complex cases, urological referral and urodynamic studies may be helpful.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Skin Breakdown and Decubitus Ulcers Pressure ulcer formation is a serious health problem in debilitated and immobilized patients. After a stroke, patients are at particular risk for pressure ulcers because they have numerous factors contributing to skin break-down. Abnormal sensation, contracture, malnutrition, immobility, and muscle and soft-­ tissue atrophy often develop and may be complicated by advanced age. Pre-vention of pressure ulcers should be the focus of care. Pre-ventive measures include frequent repositioning; keeping skin clean and dry; maintaining an adequate level of nutri-tion; and in high-­risk patients, using pressure-­relief mat-tresses. 143 After pressure ulcers have formed, in addition to strictly observing the preventive and pressure relieving measures previously noted, treatments include meticulous wound care with a variety of agents and possibly surgical reconstruction.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Dysphagia Swallowing disorders are common after a stroke. Dyspha-gia is more common in elderly patients, with an incidence of 25% to 45%. 52,54 Aspiration can lead to pneumonia, and decreased oral intake can lead to dehydration and malnutrition. Screening for dysphagia should occur within the first 24 hours of hospitalization for patients with acute stroke, before oral feedings or medications are initiated (AHA stroke rehab guidelines). In patients with evidence of dysphagia on screening, a more comprehen-sive assessment of swallowing is indicated, often including either videoflouroscopic swallowing studies, or flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing. Chapter 29 covers the details of the pathology of aspiration and the methods of its treatment.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Aspiration Aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis that can lead to a secondary bacterial infection. Because numerous anaero-bic organisms colonize the mouth, aspiration pneumonia can develop into an anaerobic abscess. 116 Such abscesses occur less frequently in edentulous individuals because they have reduced oral flora; abscesses can occur in up to one third of hospitalized patients. 103 The treatment of choice is to reduce the risk of aspiration and to administer antibiotics. Examining a radiographic film for evidence of abscess cavities and the sputum for organisms can help one develop a specific medical treatment. Sputum culture growth often requires up to 3 or 4 days, so initial treat-ment is often empirical and should be the administration

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: BOX 1.3 Risk Factors for Deep Venous Thrombosis

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: of a wide-­ spectrum antibiotic that is effective against hospital-­acquired organisms (which are often resistant to certain antibiotics) and anaerobic bacteria. 116 The usual course of antibiotics is 7 to 10 days, but cavitary pneumo-nia may require far longer treatment for eradication of the organism. 100

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Deep Venous Thrombosis DVT is a common prob-­lem after stroke and has an inci-dence of 23% to 75% depending on the severity of the stroke. Most of the morbidity and mortality associated with DVT results from venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pulmonary embolism (PE) after stroke has an incidence of 10% to 29% and a mortality rate of 10%. 13 The forma-tion of DVT is caused by the triad of risk factors outlined by Virchow postulates: altered blood flow, damage to the blood vessel wall, and altered blood coagulability. Box 1.3 lists the common risk factors for DVT. Of the risk fac-tors for DVT, stasis is one of the most important. After a stroke, DVT is 10 times more common in the paretic leg. 177 DVT usually begins in the calf, and although these clots to not typically cause emboli, these thrombi propa-gate proximally in about 20% of cases, and about 50% of the proximal deep venous thrombi embolize. About 20% of symptomatic pulmonary emboli are fatal. 145 After a stroke, ambulation in itself is not preventive in the subacute setting: PE occurred in 57% of ambulatory patients in the rehabilitation setting. 163 Lower extrem-ity and pelvic DVT are the most common, but proximal upper extremity DVT also can occur, although it is rare. All of the diagnostic and management issues discussed in the section on VTE that follows apply to this condition as well. The clinical diagnosis of DVT in the clinical setting is unreliable, 13 and many patients with life-­threatening embolism and thrombosis have no local clinical symptoms of DVT in the leg. Other patients with swelling and ten-derness may not have DVT at all and may have any of a number of other diagnoses. The differential diagnosis of lower extremity pain and swelling includes trauma, frac-ture, gout, cellulitis, and superficial phlebitis. The usual clinical signs of DVT include pain and tenderness, swell-ing, the presence of Homans sign (elicited by dorsiflexion of the ankle while the knee is flexed resulting in pain in the

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: calf), superficial venous distention, a palpable cord, and fever. Some of these signs, such as Homans, are unreliable indicators. Homans sign is present in less than one third of patients with DVT and is present in half of patients without DVT. 76 Doppler ultrasonography, a noninvasive test that uses a handheld probe to detect blood flow in deep leg veins, is the most common imaging test used to detect DVT. The clinical diagnosis of PE is also unreliable, and only 30% of patients with PE have clinical DVT, even though 70% have venographic evidence of DVT. 13 The symptoms of submassive PE overlap with the symptoms of many other pulmonary conditions, including tachy-pnea, tachycardia, rales, hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, pleural effusion, general malaise, bronchospasm, and fever. In patients with massive PE with greater than 60% of the pulmonary circulation obstructed, patients are critically ill and develop heart failure and circula-tory collapse, and can die suddenly. 163 Patients with a high suspicion for pulmonary embolism are typically diagnosed with a CT angiogram, a study where con-trast is timed and targeted to evaluate the pulmonary arteries. The best approach to VTE is to prevent DVT. According to the 2018 Guidelines by the AHA and ASA, intermittent pneumatic compression devices are recom-mended for all patients with reduced mobility following a stroke. 129 Although external pneumatic calf compres-sion is commonly used in the ICU and acute care floors, it is less practical in rehabilitation settings given the need to mobilize patients frequently. Low-­molecular-­weight heparin is a commonly used alternative for DVT pro-phylaxis depending on the patient’s comorbidities, and conventional heparin is still used for prevention as well. Ambulatory patients must be able to walk at least 50 feet to have a reduction in risk of DVT, 15 but as previously stated, the risk of PE in ambulatory stroke patients is still significant 163 The length of time prophylaxis should continue is still not definite, but evidence shows that continuing prophylaxis well into the subacute phase is warranted. 13 Treatment of DVT with or without VTE requires anticoagulation in most cases, often with overlapping injections of low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) until oral anticoagulation is achieved. 80 Treatment with oral anticoagulants typically continues for approximately 6 months depending on the specifics of the clinical sce-nario. Patients who have contraindications for anticoagu-lation typically receive inferior vena cava filters instead. Of note, anticoagulation does not break down the clot. The warfarin or LMWH prevents progression of the clot and prevents new clots from forming. The initial clot is resorbed by the body over time. Surveillance imaging is not needed. The diagnosis of DVT or PE should not impact rehabilitation therapies once anticoagulation has been initiated.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: FUTURE TRENDS IN MEDICAL STROKE MANAGEMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Improved Primary Stroke Prevention

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Primary prevention of stroke remains the most important strategy to decrease morbidity and mortality from stroke. With a good understanding of the risk factors for stroke, risk factor modification can be targeted at groups and individuals who are at risk. Table 1.1 lists the preventable and nonpreventable risk factors for stroke. Many of the risk factors are shared with other forms of cardiovascu-lar disease, so the modification of stroke risk factors also decreases the risk of cardiac-­related morbidity and mortal-ity. Because of greater awareness and risk factor modifica-tion and largely through the treatment of blood pressure, a decline of greater than 50% in the stroke mortality rate has occurred in the past 20 years. 180 This decline appears to have leveled off, however, and is in some case even reversing, especially in certain ethnicities (Hispanic) and parts of the country, specifically the “Stroke Belt” of the American South 165. This troubling trend is in part due to the epidemic of obesity in the US.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Cardiac Rehabilitation for Stroke Patients

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Cardiac and vascular diseases share many risk factors with ischemic stroke. In an effort to decrease recurrent stroke, there is a movement to develop exercise and educational interventions that mirror traditional cardiac rehabilitation programs. Another driver for the modified cardiac reha-bilitation programs for stroke is the recognition that the most common cause of death in stroke survivors is actu-ally cardiac disease. 106 Studies of the potential benefits of modified cardiac rehabilitation programs for stroke are underway in different trials in Europe and North Amer-ica. 74,146 The goals of the programs are to increase activity and exercise tolerance as well as the secondary prevention of cardiovascular events, with education about risk factors, incorporating similar educational interventions to cardiac rehabilitation programs. Preliminary studies have shown good adherence and benefit in exercise tolerance in par-ticipants in pilot programs. 131 If the benefits seen in preliminary studies continue are confirmed in larger studies, medical intervention after stroke may incorporate more of these cardiac rehabilita-tion style interventions on a routine basis in order to both improve function and prevent both cardiac events and recurrent stroke.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Public Education

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The primary goal of primary and secondary prevention programs should be to educate individuals about risk fac-tors and then to teach them the way to modify their risks. During routine visits, a physician should be able to iden-tify at-­risk patients through a combination of a history and physical examination. Routine blood pressure screen-ing should be included in all evaluations, and patients

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: who have hypertension should be treated. A stroke risk profile has been assembled from the Framingham Study data and can be used by physicians 181 (e.g., to help a phy-sician decide which borderline hypertensive patients to treat). Education can start in the physician’s office and be continued by all the other health professionals with whom the patient comes into contact. If the community at large is educated about the risk factors of stroke, individu-als who are at highest risk can seek out the attention they require. This model has been implemented and supported through research such as the Agency for Health Care Policy and Research Smoking Cessation Clinical Practice Guidelines. 133

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: INTROCUCTION TO ACUTE STROKE REHABILITATION

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The neuro-­ICU may be the starting point of occupational therapy (OT) evaluation and treatment. Many patients are evaluated by an occupational therapist within 48 hours of a stroke. The ICU environment is often fast paced with the focus on monitoring the individual patient’s medical status. The primary goals of any neuro-­ICU are to stabilize the patient medically, progress the patient neurologically, and support the patient and family through this neurologic crisis. 161 Medical testing and procedures take precedence over any OT treatment. Scheduling OT services may be difficult, treatments may be interrupted, and flexibility is necessary.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: THE IMPORTANCE OF EARLY INTERVENTION

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: There are many common complications associated with a prolonged ICU stay, which include but are not limited to deconditioning, muscle weakness, contractures, skin impairments, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. 53 Early OT, engaging in ADLs and mobilization, can increase a patient’s level of consciousness, enhance overall mental well-­being, and foster functional indepen-dence. 139,161 Occupational therapists provide a variety of treatments in the ICU, including, but not limited to, evaluations, splinting, positioning, cognitive retraining, self-­care, and functional mobility training.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: TEAM APPROACH

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: There are many members of the neuro-­ICU and acute care team, and the team may vary among settings. They include a primary team of physicians led by an attending neurologist specializing in critical care. Depending on each case, neurosurgeons may also be involved in patient care. At teaching hospitals, a team of residents may also make medical decisions regarding the patients. Along with the occupational therapist, the ancillary team consists of nursing, including the primary nurse and nurse practi-tioner, social workers, nutritionist, speech and language pathologist, and physical therapist (Table 1.10). An occu-pational therapist treating patients in this environment must foster these relationships to safely treat patients. The relationship between the primary physician, nurse, and the occupational therapist is particularly important. Daily communication with the physicians, residents, and primary nurse is necessary before initiating an evaluation or treatment session because of the fluctuating physical condition in the ICU phase of hospitalization 148,3 Physicians, nurses, or the occupational therapist, using their own clinical judgment, will determine if intervention should be delayed if a patient’s neurologic status deteriorates. After the patient has been medically cleared for OT evaluation, a review of the patient’s medical chart should be completed. The therapist can glean information relating to any precautions and complications that may interfere with the OT treatment (Box 1.4).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: MONITORING THE INTENSIVE CARE UNIT AND ACUTE STROKE SURVIVOR

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Any therapist treating patients in the ICU should not only be aware of the medical and nursing priorities in the ICU but also of how to monitor the patient during OT treatment. The therapist needs to be competent in read-ing ICU monitors and handling ICU-­related drains and lines so that appropriate parameters and precautions are adhered to during the treatment session. Common moni-tors, drains, lines, and clinical implications are listed later.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Basic ICU Monitor

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Most ICU patients are connected to a monitor that allows constant display of all vital signs (Fig. 1.10). These include

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: BOX 1.4 Initiating Treatment

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: 1. Check to make sure occupational therapy (OT) orders are active. This should be done before each and every treatment session. 2. Review the patient’s medical record. The therapist should evaluate the medical record for potential reasons to hold a patient from therapy. Such reasons may be a change in mental status, development of a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, or expansion of the stroke. Every facility has different standards for when therapy is to be held. 3. Review the patient’s current status with the medical team. Using clinical reasoning, the therapist will determine if the patient is appropriate for an OT session. The therapist should clear any treatment with the patient’s nurse to determine if all medical information reviewed from the medical record is most current. 4. Begin evaluation and treatment with a gross assessment of mental status, strength, and vital signs. Great discrepancies from what is reported in the medical record should be reported to the nurse and treatment suspended. Proceed with therapy as indicated.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: blood pressure, telemetry reading (which includes heart rate and rhythm), respiratory rate, and oxygen satura-tion percentages. For normal versus abnormal vital sign responses to exercises, refer to Table 1.11. Blood pres-sure can be monitored either noninvasively (automated pressure cuff) or by invasive measures, such as an arterial line reading (also referred to as an A-­line). A common insertion site for an A-­line is either the radial or femoral artery (Fig. 1.11). With radial artery placement, passive ROM of the wrist should be avoided; with femoral artery placement, no hip ROM is allowed, resulting in bed rest.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Telemetry

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Telemetry detects both the heart rate and rhythm and displays this reading on the monitor. Bedside telemetry is similar to an ECG. An ECG is read by placing 12 electri-cal leads to read heart rate and rhythm; bedside telemetry uses either three or five leads. The primary nurse sets both heart rate and rhythm parameters on the monitor. If the rate and rhythm become abnormal, an alarm will sound. Physical activity should be monitored accordingly.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Common Lines and Drains

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Foley Catheter A Foley catheter is indwelling and is used to drain urine from the bladder. The therapist should avoid clamping the catheter; doing so could result in a backup of urine in the bladder. The bag, which collects the urine, needs to be at a lower level than the patient’s bladder for the urine to flow in the correct direction.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: External Ventricular Drain The external ventricular drain (EVD) is a small tube sur-gically inserted into the ventricles of the brain, which drains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (Fig. 1.12). The tube is connected to a device that measures the amount of this fluid. This procedure is used when the ICP is elevated, and the drain may be clamped for short periods of time by nursing only. Because of specific calibration, function of the drain, and accuracy in measurement, the head of the bed must be elevated to a specific level. Unless the drain is clamped, the head of the bed may not be changed, and patients should not be mobilized.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring Catheter The ICP monitoring catheter is passed through a burr hole and placed in the ventricles of the brain. It is used with injuries such as hemorrhages, aneurysms, or head trauma that may lead to brain swelling and elevation of the ICP. This monitor measures any changes in ICP. The head of

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: the bed is elevated to a set point (usually 30 to 45 degrees) because the ICP will increase when the head of the bed is lowered. Passive therapy, such as splinting or positioning, may be implemented with physician approval. Generally, ADL treatment and mobilization are held at this time.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Spinal Drain A spinal drain is a catheter placed in the lumbar spine to drain CSF. It can be used for the treatment of CSF leak or to drain excess CSF fluid. The lumbar drain should be set to drain below the level of the leak. When the drain is open and is draining CSF, the spinal drain is set at a determined level next to the bed. At this time, when the drain is opened, patients are placed flat on their backs to allow for drainage. Patients with this drain may get up and out of bed and may engage in ADL treatment only when the drain has been clamped by the nurse. While the drain is open to drain CSF, the patient must remain on bed rest.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Intravenous Line IV lines are inserted into the peripheral veins and are generally used to administer IV fluids and medications. Because these lines are superficial, care should be taken not to place pressure from the positioning materials or splints directly over the area in order to avoid obstructed or dislodgment.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Feeding Tubes In the event that a stroke patient is unable to swallow effectively or appears to be a high aspiration risk, alternate methods are used for nutrition intake.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Nasogastric Tube. A nasogastric tube (NGT) is placed through the nostril down the esophagus to the stomach for liquid feeds to pass. It is generally used as a short-­term alternative for nutritional intake.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy is a tube inserted surgically with an endoscope through the mouth and into the stomach, exiting out through the stomach wall and dermis (Fig. 1.13). Precautions for both feeding tubes include elevating the head of the bed to 30 degrees or greater while admin-istering the tubes to prevent aspiration. Depending on the hospital guidelines, the therapist may be allowed to turn off the feeding before the therapy session, but it is recom-mended that the primary care nurse be consulted before doing so for patient safety (see Chapter 30).
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Ventilator At times stroke can result in respiratory failure. When this is the case, patients often require a ventilator to assist them with or to perform the act of breathing for them (Figs. 1.14 and 1.15). When a ventilator is used, the patient also requires an artificial airway. In the first few days after acute stroke, a ventilator can be connected to the patient via an endotracheal tube. A breathing tube is then placed into the patient’s mouth and positioned down into the patient’s lung systems. If a patient is unable to be weaned from the ventilator, a tracheotomy will be performed. In this procedure, an opening is cut in the patient’s trachea, and a small endotracheal tube is placed in the opening, which is then attached to the vent via long tubing. Early mobilization of patients on ventilators is encouraged. 123 A randomized controlled trial 150 emphasized that early OT and physical therapy (PT) for ventilated and critically ill patients are both beneficial and safe, resulting in bet-ter functional outcomes, decreased delirium, and more ventilator-­free days. When the therapist is confident to handle the lines, leads, and monitors in the ICU, the patient’s tolerance of the OT intervention should be monitored carefully. Vital signs should be observed during the entire treatment ses-sion and should be documented at the beginning, at the midportion, and at the end of treatment. In addition to vital signs, the therapist must also watch for changes in the patient’s neurologic status during treatment, which

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: may include changes in decorticate or decerebrate postur-ing, tone, pupils, or in speech. 149 Patients’ subjective com-plaints must be considered. If any changes in the patient’s status occur, the treatment should be terminated, and the medical team should be informed immediately.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: ASSESSMENTS USED IN ACUTE STROKE REHABILITATION

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: A variety of standardized assessments are available 89 to occupational therapists in the hospital setting. In the acute or ICU setting, it is imperative for the occupational thera-pist to evaluate motor skills, cognitive function, and ADLs. At times it may not be feasible for a patient to engage in ADL tasks secondary to medical status or sedation. Table 1.12 outlines some of the standardized assessments used during acute rehabilitation.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: REHABILITATION

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The following sections describe potential interventions for patients in the ICU or acute stage of stroke rehabilitation.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Splinting

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The primary goals at this early phase of splinting are to: 1. Correct any biomechanical malalignment and protect joint integrity. 2. Prevent shortening of soft tissues and development of contractures. 3. Maintain skin integrity. An appropriate wearing schedule should be developed to prevent learned nonuse behavior patterns. Splint wear-ing at night may be more appropriate than day use, par-ticularly if the patient has begun to initiate movement or attempts to incorporate the hand or upper extremity in functional activities. A wearing schedule should be practi-cal to achieve compliance (Box 1.5; see Chapter 23).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Positioning

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Because of the medical complexity of acute stroke survivors in the ICU, many of these patients spend most, if not all, of their time confined to bed. Therefore, positioning has become an integral part of OT treatment plan. The occupa-tional therapist will work to develop a positioning schedule for each individual positioning. The occupational therapist must rely on other members of the in-­terdisciplinary team, including nursing and physical therapists, and the patient’s family members, if able, to carry out this portion of the treatment plan (Figs. 1.16 and 1.17).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Different members of the interdisciplinary team have different priorities related to positioning. A primary goal of the team in regard to positioning is to prevent skin breakdown. The occupational therapist is encouraged to teach the team how to position the patient not only to prevent skin breakdown but also to reduce the risk of con-tractures and encourage joint alignment and comfort. The occupational therapist should develop a turning schedule for each patient. Patients should alternately be positioned on the affected side, the nonaffected side, and supine. A clock drawn with specific positions can be used as a reminder for the nursing team (see Chapter 20). When the patient is being positioned, the patient’s lines and leads should be carefully observed because they provide vital medications and monitoring of each patient. Careful adjustments need to be made for head of the bed restrictions from feeding tubes or ICP/EVD. When a patient is being positioned with femoral arterial lines, care should be taken to avoid hip flexion, and the wrists of patients with radial A-­lines should be maintained in a neutral position. Foley and rectal tubes should be moved to the same side to which the patient is positioned. While in the ICU, many patients require a ventilator to provide respiratory assistance. These patients can also be positioned side to side and supine. Care should be taken when moving ventilation tubes. There are many extraar-ticular handles that allow for additional mobility of the patient on a ventilator. If these articular handles do not provide enough length to position a patient in the proper alignment, discuss with the respiratory therapist regarding switching the ventilator from side to side every other day or so.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Functional Activity Suggestions during the Acute Phase

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Bed Mobility Rolling to the Affected Side. Rolling to the affected side

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: promotes early active trunk control and may increase awareness of the weaker side.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Rolling to the Unaffected Side. Rolling to the unaffected side promotes awareness and initial management of the weak upper extremity by teaching the patient to passively guide the arm across the trunk (Fig. 1.18).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Maintaining Side Lying. A rolled pillow placed at the mid-thoracic spine to the lumbar area may assist the patient in maintaining the side-­lying position. A towel roll can be placed under the patient’s waist to provide a stretch to the shortened trunk. A primary goal is to assure proper spine alignment, to avoid pressure buildup over the bony prominences in the lower extremities (knees and ankles), and to position the scapula in protraction if the patient is positioned on the weakened side.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Bridging. Bridging strengthens the back and hip exten-

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: sors. From a functional perspective, this movement aids in

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: getting on and off the bed pan, can be used during lower-­ body dressing, and assists moving the lower body toward the side of the bed in anticipation of assuming a sitting position.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Side Lying to Sitting Toward the Affected Side. Side lying to sitting toward the affected side promotes early-­stage weight bearing on the weak upper extremity. The thera-pist needs to ensure that the shoulder is properly aligned, and the patient usually requires assistance with initiation of the movement.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Side Lying to Sitting Toward the Unaffected Side. Therapists need to be mindful that the involved shoulder remains in a forward position during the motion of side lying to sitting toward the unaffected side.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Weight Bearing for Function

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Upper extremity weight-­bearing activities may be done while the patient is side lying as mentioned previously, during bed mobility, or for stabilizing items. It can also be accomplished using the bedside table during meals or grooming tasks (see Chapter 20). The arm or backrest of a chair can be incorporated in the treatment plan for positioning and setup for weight bearing (Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). The patient should be taught to push off with both upper extremities when moving from sitting to stand-ing. Weight bearing as a postural support can reverse or prevent tissue shortening of the elbow, wrist, and finger flexors. It can also be used to strengthen the scapula mus-culature and the triceps. Arm-­extended weight bearing can be done in front of the sink during grooming or be done in front of the bedside table while reaching for items nearby (Fig. 1.21). For the lower extremity, bed-­level activities include bridging, sitting at the edge of the bed with both feet on the floor, and early transfer training when patients are medically stable.
cross_page_merge_reasons: high: following block begins with lowercase continuation text

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Graded Sitting and Standing Activities Supported Sitting in Bed. For the supported sitting in bed position, the head of the bed should gradually be raised in approximately 30-­ to 40-­degree increments to avoid an orthostatic hypotensive response. As the patient tolerates the change in degrees of elevation, the therapist should continue to monitor vital signs. If there appears to be no change in the patient’s blood pressure, the therapist should continue to elevate the head of the bed to approximately 80 degrees. Sit-ting at a slightly reclined position is less taxing on the patient’s energy and requires less recruitment of the neck, trunk, and back musculature to maintain an upright position. At this point, the patient should be engaged in functional activities, such as feeding, light grooming, upper-­body bathing and dressing, and lei-sure activities.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Supported Sitting in a Chair. If the patient is well sup-ported and can endure sitting in a chair at the bedside, “sitting tolerance” or “out of bed tolerance” can be increased. Pillows may be useful at this early stage to sup-port the lumbar spine and weaker upper extremity. When a therapist is placing a pillow under the upper extremity, he or she should make sure the shoulder alignment is in neutral. Adequate postural support may reduce pain and fatigue. The focus of treatment can include but is not lim-ited to the patient performing self-­care tasks, visual scan-ning activities, and weight bearing through the upper and lower extremity.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Unsupported Sitting. Unsupported sitting may be done in the bed in a “tailor” (crossed-­legged) position, depend-ing on the amount of ROM the patient has in the lower extremities. The head of the bed can be elevated but should not touch the back of the patient. It is used as a safety catch if the patient loses his or her balance in a pos-terior direction. Pillows may be propped against the bed rails to protect the patient if he or she leans or falls later-ally to the weaker side. While seated in this position, the patient can practice righting himself or herself or main-taining a midline position, and the patient should then be engaged in functional activities as tolerated.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Unsupported Sitting at the Edge of the Bed with Feet Dan-gling. In this position, the patient can be challenged with

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: increased demands on alignment, trunk control, and for-ward and lateral weight shifts. Scooting to the edge of the bed can be introduced in anticipation of progressing to sit to stand. Postural control may be noticeably improved when the patient’s feet contact the floor. The therapist should ensure equal weight bearing on both lower extrem-ities (see Chapter 7).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Sit to Stand: Pretransfer Phase. To prepare for the sit-­ to-­stand pretransfer phase, therapists should ensure that all lines and IVs have enough length to eliminate pulling or tension. Increasing the surface height the patient rises from will require less work. This transition may require the assistance of more than one person to gain the patient’s confidence and safety. The therapist should assure appro-priate alignment of both lower extremities with feet placed firmly on the floor and then have the patient begin with several partial sit-­to-­stand trials. Assess how the weaker lower extremity reacts to weight bearing, provide appro-priate blocking or support to prevent collapse, and check vital signs while the patient is upright.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Supported Standing in Front of a Raised Bed. To initiate sup-ported standing in front of a raised bed, the therapist should position the patient in a chair that faces the side of the bed. With appropriate assistance, the therapist should stand the patient and sit in a chair on the patient’s weakened side to support the hip and knee extensors. In this standing position, the patient may practice early weight shifting through the lower extremities and bear weight on the upper extremities in either forearm or arm-­extended positions (Fig. 1.21).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: EDEMA MANAGEMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Evaluate the potential cause if edema is present. Discuss with nursing whether the swelling may be associated with the presence of a blood clot or an IV infiltrate. Check to see if the patient’s limb is cool or warm to the touch, observe the skin color, and assess the firmness of the swell-ing (soft, fluidlike, or pitting). In the ICU, the preferred method for treating edema is positional elevation because compression garments or ace wraps may not be appropriate because of various IVs and line access needed by nursing. The extended limb should be positioned above the heart. Active or active assistive ROM should be encouraged and followed by manual mas-sage (Fig. 1.22; see Chapter 22).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: SHOULDER MANAGEMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Many patients may experience upper extremity edema, pain, humeral head subluxation, or impingement after a stroke (see Chapter 20). Many of the upper extremity interventions provided in the ICU or acute stage are pro-phylactic measures to prevent these problems. To protect the shoulder against potential pain and subluxation, the team should be educated in proper roll-ing techniques and bed mobility so they can avoid pulling on the extremity. The team should be instructed to roll the patient by placing the hands on the trunk rather than pulling on the extremity. Signage can be hung behind the patient’s bed indicating that the patient may have shoul-der subluxation and informing the team to not pull on the patient’s arm (Box 1.6).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: BOX 1.6 Patient with Right Shoulder Subluxation

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Please do not pull on the patient’s arm. Please contact occupational therapy at 555-­8724 with questions or concerns.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Because of the medical complexity of ICU or acute patients, most do not get out of bed to the chair for pro-longed periods or engage in prolonged upright activities. While supine, out of bed in a chair, or dangling at the bedside, support for a weak shoulder can be provided via proper positioning.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Supine

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Support should be provided to the affected upper extrem-ity with pillows, towels, or both. The occupational ther-apist must use clinical judgment to determine proper positioning for each patient. However, as a general rule, the affected scapula should be protracted, the arm in a forward position, with the wrist neutral and fingers extended. 20

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Edge of Bed

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The affected upper extremity is supported on the bedside table or on numerous pillows.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Out of Bed in a Chair

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The affected upper extremity is supported on the bedside table, on numerous pillows, or on the arm support of the chair. Most ICU or acute patients do not require supple-mental shoulder supports such as sling, clavicle strap, or taping. These supports may be used when patients are performing ADL upright and are spending more time out of bed (see Chapter 20). In addition to positioning, the occupational therapist will provide the ICU patient with passive and active ROM and will engage the affected upper extremity in functional tasks. The therapist should mind lines and leads while providing these services. When an A-­line is present in the radial artery, wrist flexion and extension should be avoided.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: INCREASING SPATIAL AWARENESS BY ARRANGING THE ENVIRONMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Although the ICU environment may be more restrictive than a rehabilitation setting, there are subtle yet important interventions that can be implemented to increase spatial awareness. Strategically place items of common use, such as the television remote control, on the involved side while providing cues to assist the patient in locating them. Stra-tegically place food items on the meal tray during feeding to encourage scanning and locating desired items to eat. Verbal cues should be diminished as the patient’s aware-ness increases. Reverse the position of the bed, if able, so that the patient’s involved space is stimulated (e.g., facing the hallway instead of facing a blank wall). Position the bedside table and phone on the neglected or weaker side of the patient. Use brightly colored bands tied to the bed-side rails on the involved side as cues to attend to this side. Hang pictures of family and friends on the involved side while providing cues for the patient to locate them.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: EARLY COGNITIVE MANAGEMENT

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Patients may spend numerous days to weeks in the ICU. A well-­ known phenomenon called ICU psychosis can develop within days of being admitted to the ICU. 146,108 ICU psychosis has been defined as a fluctuating state of consciousness characterized by fatigue, distraction, confusion, disorientation, restlessness, clouding of con-sciousness, incoherence, fear, anxiety, excitement, halluci-nations, and delusions. 35 Many factors related to the ICU environment can contribute to the development of ICU psychosis. Some include psychosocial stress, sleep depri-vation, sensory overload or underload, and immobiliza-tion. 35 Many patients are unable to differentiate between day and night secondary to lighting in most ICUs. 35 The occupational therapist can assist the primary nurs-ing team in a variety of ways to help lessen the effects of ICU psychosis. Some measures that nursing may imple-ment are providing tactile and verbal stimulation, involve-ment of the patient in his or her care, and supplying effective rest periods. 108 The occupational therapist can minimize environmental monotony and mobilize and engage the patient in familiar self-­care tasks. When pro-viding a patient with OT services, communication with patient via gentle touch and voices can help calm patients. Incorporating music and massage into OT treatments can also help reduce anxiety, fear, and depression. 108 See Box 1.7 for treatment ideas.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: SKIN PROTECTION AND PREVENTION OF BREAKDOWN

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Skin breakdown and development of pressure ulcers are common complications associated with an ICU or acute admission. After stroke, patients are at risk for develop-ing pressure ulcers because of prolonged bed rest and immobility. Other risk factors include poor circulation, poor nutrition, edema, low level of arousal, confusion, and incontinence. 4 Pressure management and skin protection should become a part of each treatment session. See Table 1.13 for a review of the stages of pressure ulcers. Prevention of skin breakdown is a team responsibility. The occupational therapist has a unique set of skills to assist the team in protecting the patient’s skin. The occu-pational therapist is often the first team member to mobi-lize the patient and can observe the entire body for signs of skin breakdown. Areas of concern for the ICU patient include the sacrum, occiput, heels, greater trochanter, and

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: elbows. The therapist can suggest elbow and heel pads to protect these areas from pressure and friction. Heels can also be floated via positioning or multipodis boots (Fig. 1.23). The therapist can develop positioning devices to assist the nurse with elevating pressure on the occiput (Fig. 1.24) and the sacrum. The occupational therapist can also recommend specialized mattresses to best serve the patient’s needs.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: COMMUNICATION

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: For patients who are unable to communicate verbally, whether because of mechanical ventilation or aphasia, alternative methods of communication are necessary. Options may include use of a communication board. Single word choices or pictures that represent feelings or needs can be placed strategically on a small poster board. Exam-ples may include Nurse, Doctor, Pain, Thirst, and so on, to which the patient can then point. Alphabet boards are generally not used because they require energy and time for the patient to “spell” words. For patients with aphasia, words might be eliminated altogether. Other alternatives may include signals for yes-­or-­no questions, such as head nodding or thumbs up or down, and an eye blink system. Working in conjunction with the speech-­language pathol-ogist, the occupational therapist may assist with facilitat-ing a communication system that is consistently used by other staff and family members (Box 1.8; see Chapter 28).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: DYSPHAGIA SCREENING

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Acute swallowing difficulties or dysphagia are often associated with stroke. 172 The risk of aspiration is high and often leads to pneumonia. Other medical complica-tions associated with dysphagia include malnutrition and dehydration. During the initial admission to the hospital, patients may be placed on “NPO” (nothing by mouth) precau-tions. Under these circumstances, an NGT is usually inserted through the nose and down the esophagus to the stomach. If the patient is conscious, the occupational therapist may initiate a swallowing or dysphagia screening at the bedside. Before beginning the assessment, the therapist should be aware of the patient’s level of alertness, fatigue, and ability to follow commands because these factors may significantly influence the ability to participate safely. An

If an oral suction device is available at the bedside, it should be turned on (Box 1.9; Fig. 1.25). paragraphs.text: • Request the patient to stick out his or her tongue. Does it drift or deviate to one side? Can the patient lick his or her lips and perform lateral movements with the tongue?

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: • Use a tongue depressor to assess the patient’s gag reflex. Is it present, absent, or delayed?

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: • Check the soft palate. Use a flashlight to ask the patient to open mouth and say the word “ah.” Observe for soft palate elevation

paragraphs.text: • Can the patient demonstrate a volitional cough? Assess the strength of the cough. Is it adequate to clear the airway?

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: • Is the patient managing his or her own secretions? Does the patient choke or cough on his or her own secretions? Observe whether the swallow is present or delayed

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: SELF-­CARE TRAINING

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Training in ADLs is an integral part of OT treatment. It is important to engage patients in self-­care tasks as soon as they are medically stable.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Energy expenditure is often an issue for low-­ level patients, so grading the self-­care task is as important as the choice of activity. Acute patients may also be limited by IVs, lines, and artificial ventilation. If the patient is having difficulty managing secretions, begin by teaching him or her how to use an oral suctioning device. Using an adapted call light to request assistance from nursing is also an appropriate goal. For those with limited motor return, the upper extrem-ity should at least be used as a stabilizer. ADL compensa-tory strategies can be initiated. If the patient demonstrates active movement, the upper extremity should be incorpo-rated into the self-­care task (see Chapter 6). The initial position may be with the head of the bed elevated. This position provides support of the head and trunk. Vital signs should be monitored throughout the activity. As patients progress, they might be posi-tioned in sitting at the edge of the bed. Demands are greater because patients must maintain their balance while performing the task. When a patient is able to tolerate sitting at the edge of the bed, the progression should lead to performing tasks seated in a chair. If the patient is able to stand for short periods, then appro-priate self-­care activities should be performed in stand-ing, such as brushing teeth at the sink or combing hair. Chaining the tasks together demands more tolerance. Self-­care tasks can be graded from simple to complex (Box 1.11).

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: FAMILY TRAINING

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: The primary purpose of family training in the ICU or acute setting is to allow for the patient to engage in as many therapeutic activities as possible immediately after the neurologic event. Family members should be empow-ered to assist their loved ones to achieve their therapy goals. Occupational therapists may spend as much time educating the family as they do treating the patients. When training family members, the therapist should demonstrate the tasks and then provide an opportunity for the family members to attempt the tasks. Positive feedback should be provided with corrections given as needed. Families should be provided with written instruc-tions for any tasks they are asked to carry out. During one OT session, no more than three tasks should be given to the family members. This will ensure greater carryover of the tasks provided. The following are suggestions for a family training scheduled in the ICU or acute setting (see Chapter 14). Occupational therapists must use their clinical reason-ing when providing family training. Many ICU or acute care patients are too medically complex for the fam-ily to provide additional therapy services. Such patients may require constant monitoring during physical activ-ity; other patients may have lines and leads that require a nurse or therapist to handle.

paragraphs.text: After evaluation of patients, family members should be instructed in the following.

paragraphs.text: • Safely moving noncomplex lines and leads. These may be noninvasive such as a blood pressure cuff; an O 2 monitor; an IV line; and, in certain cases, A-­lines.

paragraphs.text: engaged in the treatment and trained in the following areas:

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: • Shoulder management: Families must be educated in positioning of the involved upper extremity in bed, dur-ing bed mobility, for transfers, during ADL activities, and while upright. Family members can be instructed to don and doff shoulder supports if needed.

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: • ADL training: Family members can be trained in setting up the environment using the bedside table, giving simple verbal cues, and providing physical cues to engage the affected upper extremity. If the patient is to go home directly from the acute care setting, family training of both compensatory and remedial techniques for ADL trainings should be initiated.

paragraphs.text: • Shoulder ROM: After family members are educated on how to safely handle a subluxed shoulder, they can also be educated to passively range the affected shoul-der to 90 degrees of forward flexion. In some cases, occupational therapists can use their clinical judg-ment and teach the family to perform overhead ROM if they can maintain proper alignment of the head of the humerus.

paragraphs.text: • Positioning: After the family members are edu-cated in upper extremity positioning, they should be involved in the patient’s positioning schedule. A physically able family member should be trained in proper body mechanics during bed positioning. If a family member is unable to physically complete the positioning him-­ or herself, he or she should be educated on the turning schedule and proper posi-tioning. paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: Ischemic Stroke: Management of Acute Case and Complications with Workup G.H. is a 76-­year-­old woman who has a history of hyper-tension and diabetes mellitus and had an MI 2 years ago. She arrives at her local ED 4 hours after an acute onset of weakness in her left arm and leg. She fell at home after try-ing to get up, and it was only after her neighbors heard her calls for help that the emergency services rescue team came to her aid. On admission to the emergency department, she has an elevated blood pressure of 200/100 mm Hg and is alert and oriented. Her initial physical examination reveals left-­sided weakness and sensory loss that is greater in her arm than her leg. The ED team has the impression that she has an acute stroke in evolution, so an emergency CT scan is ordered. The initial blood work and ECG are unremarkable. While she is in the CT scanner, the on-­ call resident is paged and asked to come see her because the radiology technician notes that she has become unable to move while in the machine. She now has a dense left hemiplegia. Because of fear of stroke progression, she is admitted to the ICU. Review of the CT scan shows some mild effacement of the sulci on the right side of the brain and no other clear abnormalities. The neurologic consultant advises that G.H.’s treatment that night be conservative and sup-portive and recommends that G.H. be given an enteric-­ coated aspirin each day. By the next morning, she has had no further progression of her symptoms but has flaccid left hemiplegia and hemineglect. She remains medically stable during the next several days but is unable to achieve adequate oral intake and has to have an NGT placed for enteral feeding. A physiatric consultation is obtained, and

paragraphs.text: consultation. At this point, the occupational therapist may communicate his or her clinical observations on the patient’s progress since admission to the acute care setting.

paragraphs.text: SUMMARY

paragraphs.chapter_title: Stroke Diagnosis, Acute Treatment, Prevention, and Medical Management
paragraphs.text: In summary, acute stroke rehabilitation is multifaceted. Interventions focus on prevention of secondary compli-cations, such as learned nonuse, contracture, and aspira-tion, and on early attempts at remediation of impairments. Two overarching goals include maximizing participation in appropriate ADLs and acting with the team to assure proper discharge planning.

Another CT scan is performed on the third hospital day, which reveals a clear, acute infarct in the right tem-poroparietal area with associated edema and no mass effect or hemorrhage, so the neurologist recommends an extended workup. Carotid Doppler images are normal, and the ECG indicates stability, but the echocardiogram reveals that G.H. has a decreased ejection fraction of 25% with a visible apical thrombus in the area of her previous MI. The neurologist and cardiologist concur on anticoag-ulation with heparin followed by conversion to warfarin. Anticoagulant therapy is initiated, and aspirin is no longer administered. On the sixth hospital day, G.H. is started successfully on warfarin, her hemiparesis has improved, and she is able to move her leg against gravity and with gravity elimi-nated. However, she is still unable to swallow safely and still has an NGT. G.H. is accepted for inpatient rehabili-tation and is transferred to the rehabilitation service on the eighth hospital day. G.H.’s rehabilitation course is notable because of swelling and pain in her left leg, which is found by duplex Doppler scanning to result from a DVT. Because she developed the thrombosis while receiving adequate anti-coagulation medication, she has an umbrella filter placed in her inferior vena cava to prevent development of a pul-monary embolus. G.H. becomes severely depressed, and after consultation with the psychiatry service, she begins receiving antidepressant medication, which has good results. G.H. progresses in therapy, but her left shoulder becomes painful because of a shoulder–hand syndrome, which responds well to aggressive therapeutic interven-tion. She also develops a progressive increase in skeletal muscle activity, particularly in her left hand, which can only be kept under control with aggressive ROM exer-cises. At the time of her discharge, she is able to move short distances with a hemiwalker and needs assistance with dressing her lower extremities and setting up for her basic ADLs. paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic Stroke: Management of Acute Case with Workup C.C. is a 25-­year-­old man who works as a sales man-ager in a local retail store. While dismissing a store clerk whom he caught stealing from the store safe, he suddenly complains of a severe headache, sinks to the chair in his office, and slumps over to the right. Within a few min-utes, he is unconscious, and the staff calls an ambulance. C.C. is admitted to the ED within 20 minutes, accompa-nied by the fired clerk who is proclaiming loudly that she has done nothing to him. In the ED, C.C. is in a deep coma, breathing deeply, and has dilated pupils and absent reflexes. He is intubated immediately for airway protec-tion and is taken for an emergency CT scan. The study is not completed because C.C. has a seizure while in the CT scanner, but the partially completed study shows a great deal of blood in the ventricles. C.C. is diagnosed with a presumed SAH, and treatment is started. Hyperventila-tion and treatment with mannitol begin. An ICP monitor is inserted, and C.C. is given phenytoin and nimodip-ine.
